items.contentHtml:
Please enjoy this transcript of my third interview with Henry Shukman, an authorized Zen master in the Sanbo Zen lineage, one of only a few dozen in the world, and spiritual director emeritus of Mountain Cloud Zen Center in Santa Fe, New Mexico.

Legal conditions/copyright information

Listen onApple Podcasts
Listen onOvercast
Zen Master Henry Shukman on Love and Grief, Jhana 101, Ambition, and Poetry as a Shortcut

Additional podcast platforms

Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts, , Overcast, Podcast Addict, Pocket Casts, Castbox, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Audible, or on your favorite podcast platform.

Transcripts may contain a few typos. With many episodes lasting 2+ hours, it can be difficult to catch minor errors.

Tim Ferriss: Henry, lovely to see you.

Henry Shukman: Great to see you, Tim.

Tim Ferriss: In the flesh. And it has been a hot minute since we had a proper podcast episode like this. 2001 was the last. Before we get to that, for people who don’t have the context, would you mind giving a brief bio?

Henry Shukman: Sure thing. Yeah. I mean, we could eat up the whole thing happily. Be careful. But yeah, I’m a Zen teacher and a meditation teacher more generally, and I’m a writer and poet. I am from the UK, as you can probably tell by my accent, but I have lived in Santa Fe, New Mexico, for more or less the last 35 years, or 30 years. And so, I make my home there.

Tim Ferriss: All right. Well, since you’re giving us the abbreviated version, which I appreciate, we’re going to dig into certain aspects of that. Let’s start with a question that is not on the expected menu, which is, why Santa Fe?

I’m sure people would be like, “Wait a second. Okay. You had me. UK, poet. Okay. Check. UK Zen teacher. Okay. Well, maybe okay. We’ve heard of Alan Watts, and this, that, and the other thing. It may be okay.” And then they’re like, “Wait, Santa Fe? Why Santa Fe, New Mexico?”

Henry Shukman: I’ll tell you, when I was a teenager, I got into D.H. Lawrence, who was riding high in those days. He had a very high stature in the literary pantheon back then, which he probably doesn’t really have anymore. People might not even have heard of him. He’s most notorious for Lady Chatterley’s Lover, which was a banned book, way back in the day in 1929.

But he was a really unusual English writer, in that he was incredibly adventurous. He broke all the rules of society and of literature. He wrote some incredible poems and some incredible books, along with a lot of stuff that we might not really want to read today, maybe.

But he had a sort of life of wandering, which I found incredibly appealing. He never really lived anywhere. But the one place that he actually owned a house was New Mexico. And actually it was given to him, which is how he came to own it.

Tim Ferriss: That’s how he ended up with it.

Henry Shukman: He wrote about New Mexico incredibly beautifully and evocatively and vividly. And I remember reading, there’s a little book of his called Mornings in Mexico, which is both about Mexico and New Mexico. Some of the descriptions of being around Taos in Northern New Mexico near Santa Fe, were just so kind of thrilling and powerful. They got my blood really seething to read them. I always wanted to go there. When I was a young man, I’d actually wrote my first book, quite inspired by that, by Lawrence, when I was 19.

Tim Ferriss: Stylistically.

Henry Shukman: More sort of—I was going to say spiritually, but that’s not exactly right. Because what he does in that book, Mornings in Mexico, is he evokes places with incredible power and potency, so that you really feel viscerally what it was like, at least for him to be there. You sort of get almost a transfusion of the place. I was just blown away by that. And so, when I was 18, 19, I went away to work abroad, actually in Argentina, the other side of the world from the UK.

Tim Ferriss: How did I not know all these things about you? This is crazy. We’ve had so many conversations. I’m so glad that I decided to ask you about New Mexico. All right.

Henry Shukman: And so, after working in Argentina with a good old buddy of mine, we were traveling together, we put on our backpacks and we hiked, and we hiked out of this ranch we’d been working on, this farm we’d been on, to the end of the road and hitchhiked north into Bolivia, and spent two and a half months or so basically traveling around this, they call it the Altiplano, this high table land, 13,000 feet high, of Bolivia.

Tim Ferriss: That’s high. Yeah.

Henry Shukman: With Aymara Indians on it, and mind-blowingly beautiful, and basically actually no travelers. It wasn’t on the Gringo Trail, as they called it, that backpackers know.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, 13,000 feet.

Henry Shukman: That’ll put a lot of people off, and very remote. I wrote a book and this buddy I was with took photographs, and we were going to do a book. We were only 19. But the point I was going to make is that on that trip writing that book, I wanted to try my best to do what I felt Lawrence was doing in that book, Mornings in Mexico, which was evoke the place that you were in through your writing.

I’d been writing poetry since I was a young teen, and reading and devouring poetry. I was just sort of a literary fiend. I didn’t know to whatever extent I could do it, but I felt sometimes I could feel something moving in me. It was thrilling. And actually that book got published a few years later.

And that then led to my doing another book, which I was also a musician. I went to play my trombone around the Caribbean in different bands, soca bands, calypso bands, reggae bands, et cetera, salsa, for a year, and I wrote a book about that. Then my publishers then said, “We want another book. What do you want to do?”

At the time I was in New York, actually, I’d been playing with a band there, and you didn’t know this about my musical life as well. But anyway, that’s when I thought, “Oh, my gosh. I want to go to New Mexico. I’m at least in the right country right now.” And so, I proposed that, and they said, “Great, go ahead.” I went out to New Mexico to sort of see what was left of D.H. Lawrence’s—

Tim Ferriss: Did you go directly to Taos, or did you end up—

Henry Shukman: I did not. I did not. I first went to this little place called Cloudcroft, which is in the south.

Tim Ferriss: It’s a cool name.

Henry Shukman: Yeah. It’s right down in the south of New Mexico, where a friend of a friend had a trailer that they said I could go stay in.

Tim Ferriss: Into the wild.

Henry Shukman: Exactly.

Tim Ferriss: Don’t eat the mushrooms.

Henry Shukman: And so, I stayed there for a bit, and I realized, this isn’t the New Mexico that D.H. Lawrence wrote about. It was more like ranching and alpine forest. It was four hours south of Taos. Eventually, after actually a couple of weeks there, I thought, “I’ve got to go to Lawrence’s part.”

Tim Ferriss: So, hold on. Hold on. I’m just going to pause here. I’m just imagining, you’ve built up this expectation over decades, or to whatever it is, a decade, let’s just say, however many years. Did you feel when you first got there, and you were walking up to this trailer, and you’re like, “Wait a second. This hamburger looks nothing like that photograph that I see up on the wall at McDonald’s.”

I mean, was there a level of, “Oh, shit,” disappointment? Or were you just bewildered by the difference between what D.H. Lawrence described and what you were experiencing? Or was there none of that? You were just like, “Oh. Interesting.”

Henry Shukman: Yeah. No, it’s a good question. I think basically I was so thrilled to be in a new place. I was a hungry traveler in those early years, so it was just great to be somewhere new. And so gradually it dawned on me, “Hey, this isn’t quite like what he saw.” It wasn’t desert, because there were all ranches around there, and there was a big Air Force base nearby. It was really a very different scene.

And so, it slowly sank in, “This isn’t the place that he was at, which is what I’m really after.” So then I got on a bus, a Greyhound bus, which took me to Albuquerque, four hours north. Then I got on another bus in Albuquerque to Taos. I was there for probably two months, initially. I rented a little room, and I didn’t have a car, so I had to have a place that was close enough to town that I could walk to shop.

Tim Ferriss: I was going to say, “Welcome to America.”

Henry Shukman: That was a shock.

Tim Ferriss: Not exactly a great subway in Taos, I’m imagining.

Henry Shukman: But it was fantastic to be there. God, with adobe architecture and that huge mountain of Taos just sitting there, getting to know some folks from Taos Pueblo, Indigenous people. You know what the weird thing was? It was so unlike what I knew, and yet there was a weird sense of similarity, almost, because it was fields and trees, and often actually the weather was a little bit cloudy, because it’s mountainous.

I remember having this strange feeling like, it’s not that different from the English countryside that I grew up loving. I went wandering the hills and fields around our home in the country when I was a young teen, and especially in summer. The feeling wasn’t actually that different. I had a strange kind of almost deja vu between the Taos countryside and the English countryside.

And it seems really farfetched, but actually no, there really is something in just the sort of tussocky grass and the sort of scruffy fields. Yeah, it was great to get to feel that I was where this former literary idol of mine lived.

Tim Ferriss: At that point, were you still in the midst of high gear with poetry?

Henry Shukman: I was [inaudible 00:13:53]—

Tim Ferriss: Because It seems like at some point, you exit stage left. I think at least certainly from chatting with your friend David Whyte, you’re understating your accomplishments and trajectory with poetry a bit, when you introduced yourself.

But it seems like maybe you, it seems kind of abrupt, I don’t know, kind of exited stage left as I put it, away from poetry and then a lot has happened since our last conversation, and then poetry has always been a part of your life, but it seems to have come even more full force back into the fold.

But when you were in New Mexico at that point, were you still writing poetry? Or were you completely shifted to writing more prose in book form?

Henry Shukman: Poetry was always kind of going along in the background. And so, it was still happening then. But, yeah, I mean, I was actually making my living from prose books then. So, yeah, I ended up writing a book about New Mexico called Savage Pilgrims, which was about this sort of search for the traces of D.H. Lawrence in New Mexico, and meeting a ton of interesting people along the way.

But what David Whyte was talking about, there was a point when I had quite a busy career as a poet.

Tim Ferriss: Which is not a sentence you hear very often.

Henry Shukman: No. It was really unusual. It’s true. I mean, I had this little phase of being really kind of lucky when I won a number of prizes, some of them quite big. This was in the UK. And a great publisher, and lots of invitations to go and read around the country. And actually, that morphed into—

I mean, I don’t want to drag you too much through the whole trajectory. It gets a bit boring. But I also started writing fiction as well, and publishing that. But then there was a point where I stopped. I stopped that writing trajectory. It’s true. That’s what David was talking about. Because I’d had this Zen thing going on all along as well, for decades by then.

Tim Ferriss: Okay. All along?

Henry Shukman: Well, since the age of 24, I’d been meditating very regularly. And at a certain point, I got more serious about the Zen.

Tim Ferriss: What triggered the getting more serious?

Henry Shukman: Finding a teacher. Finding a teacher that I really wanted to study with, which I’d never imagined actually that I would do.

Tim Ferriss: Was that a chance encounter? Because it seems like if you wanted to find a teacher, maybe you presumably could have done it earlier. Did the teacher just show up like Obi-Wan Kenobi, or how did it materialize?

Henry Shukman: Thanks for asking. But I think that I sort of had been trying to find a teacher, but rather unconsciously. I’d been going to lots of different centers for years, doing retreats with them, and getting a meeting with a teacher. I didn’t really think that I was looking for a teacher, but I wanted to get in somehow deeper into it.

Tim Ferriss: Into the practice.

Henry Shukman: Into the practice. But every time I went somewhere, I would feel, “Eh. I don’t want to join them. I’m happy to come and do something with them, but I don’t want to be part of this.” I wasn’t the kind of guy who happily just joined some weird band of people doing this sort of strange meditation thing. As a writer, that’s not for me. So, I wouldn’t actually join. I’d sort of go and do a retreat, and clear out afterwards.

Tim Ferriss: Cameo.

Henry Shukman: Yeah, exactly.

Tim Ferriss: Until—

Henry Shukman: But then, yeah. There was a center in my hometown, Oxford, where I was back. I had a fellowship in Oxford for a couple of years, so I was back there for that. That was the town I grew up in in England, and there was a Zen center there, and I was going to it. I’d slip in just before they started, and I’d be the first person out at the end of the weekly sits they had.

And one day I went early, because you could sit in the afternoon if you wanted to, to get a bit more sitting in. I happened to run into the teacher in the corridor of this house where they had the Zen center. I was on my way to the loo and hoping—but there he was, and accidentally engaged me in conversation.

Tim Ferriss: Trapped.

Henry Shukman: It was how can I get out? Anyway, we ended up having a cup of tea and chatting. In the course of that conversation at the kitchen table of the little zendo with a cup of tea, I just realized, “God, I want to tell this guy more about my practice,” because he wanted to know and I wanted to share it with him.

He asked simple questions like, “Why are you here? What are you doing this practice for?” Which actually, funny, nobody had asked me that before. And he really understood when I answered those questions. He was an ordinary guy. He wasn’t wearing robes. He’d retired quite young.

Tim Ferriss: No scepter.

Henry Shukman: No scepter. No orb or scepter. No stick. He’s just a fleece, an ordinary guy. He’d retired young from being a lawyer. He was running two charities, and he was into Zen. What I loved about it was, A, he was just normal, no dressing up in robes, or any of that nonsense. But also, when you were chatting with him, he was normal, and yet he could go totally deep.

Just because he was chatting normally didn’t mean that he didn’t know these vast depths that Zen can open up. He totally did. So, when I described a certain experience that I’d had, which had got me curious about Zen in the first place, he instantly understood. And it wasn’t just like he spoke like he understood it. I could feel, he really got it.


Just for context, I’d had a random, spontaneous, out of nowhere awakening experience when I was 19. I didn’t know that’s what it was. But I’d had this sudden flash that was very powerful, of discovering that my ordinary way of understanding myself as this being that lives in this body somehow, that’s separate from everything outside it, that collapsed, and I felt that I was part of everything, boundlessly, truly everything.

I was totally sober at the time. I hadn’t had any psychedelics. I wasn’t interested actually in anything like that, nor was I interested in discovering boundless unity with the cosmos. I wasn’t interested in it, but I suddenly found it. I mean, that’s not it. It fell upon me, or something. I don’t know exactly how to put it. But I just saw my immediate experience in a totally different way, which I knew was more real than the way I ordinarily saw it.

Now, it was incredibly beautiful, and it left a marvelous sort of wake afterwards for several weeks, when I felt weightless and clear, and my heart was filled with something like love, or some beautiful sensation. I can actually almost palpably feel this, like a sort of fountain silently welling up in my—I was giving you a lot now. But it was an incredibly powerful experience for me.

And six weeks later, this was at the end of that trip I was talking about, where I wrote my first book in South America. Six weeks later or so, I went home and had a really awful reentry with a kind of breakdown, although I didn’t know it was that at the time, but it was sort of hellish.

Tim Ferriss: Do you think that was connected to the awakening experience, in some way?

Henry Shukman: I do. I do. And I think it works like how—

Tim Ferriss: It was good news, bad news.

Henry Shukman: It is. It is, really. I mean, in a way, it’s all good news, sort of, because I think basically what had happened in that awakening experience, is that I’d grown up with complex childhood trauma, but I didn’t know that either. I’d also developed a lot of adaptations sort of thing of personality, to defend against the trauma, so I didn’t have to feel it, because it was overwhelming.

When I got back home, after that awakening experience, I was very open, and I basically shed those defenses and adaptations. And I remember I was lying in the bath. I’d come back. Actually, I’d gone to my dad’s house, not my mom’s house, as it so happened when I first got back. Got the bus from the airport, he picked me up, took me home. And I was lying in the bath upstairs, and I was hearing his voice and my stepmother’s voice down in the kitchen downstairs, and it was suddenly—

It’s like this weird layer of deep familiarity, hearing those voices, hearing the sounds of the plumbing in the house. And it was like I was back in an old nightmare that I’d never recognized as the nightmare that it was. But now that I was open because of that experience, I recognized it, and I was just overwhelmed by grief, and I started crying. And at that point, I realized I hadn’t cried in 10 years, not since my father left home when I was seven, 12 years, because I’d been so shut down.

So the awakening experience had totally opened me up, which, given the right support and context, is such a powerful healing thing. And I think this is the way awakening can work, that it opens us up, and therefore healing can happen. But I had absolutely zero understanding of any of this, age 19, about to go to Cambridge to do a challenging degree that I was all pumped up and wanted to do.

But right then, it was like a crippling blow of this catastrophic event of my inner life collapsing. And I felt that I’d lost the experience of—I wouldn’t have called it awakening, but whatever that beautiful thing that had happened to me, I’d lost it, and it was my fault. I’d been an idiot. I’d come home. I shouldn’t have come home. I’d walked back into hell. Hell would never let me out again.

I mean, it felt like the worst possible thing that could have happened, really. And it was my fault. So, a ton of shame around this, and it was really hard. I had a very hard few years. I managed to finish at Cambridge. I did much less well than I probably could have done, and it was a very uncomfortable experience, all in all.

Then when I was blessedly introduced to meditation by two friends, and I started doing TM, which I know you know as well, it was a game-changer. Because suddenly I had something at least that was introducing a little bit of nervous system regulation to my totally unregulated, dysregulated, highly anxious or depressed nervous system. Then from that, I got into therapy, and I sort of began to piece together a path of healing.

But to your point about when I met this guy, John, he’s called John Gaynor, this Zen teacher, the first thing he asked me is, “Why are you here?” I started answering some sort of bullshit about liking to meditate and stuff, and I stopped myself. I said, “Really, why am I here?” It was because of that experience when I was 19, of the world embracing me, or however to put it. I told him that.

And when I told him that, I don’t know exactly how to convey it. I knew he understood. And I was absolutely right. I mean, I didn’t know it then, but I found out later, of course, he’d had something similar, and more. Because what I also didn’t know, was that what I’d experienced then wasn’t the end of the road. It sort of felt like an ultimate revelation. But actually, what’s so incredible, if you get into a deep track like Zen can be, there’s more, and he was able to guide me to more. Yeah.

Tim Ferriss: I guess there’s the recognition that you had, which was this St. Nicholas twinkle in the eye, or whatever he had, right? The knowing. And I don’t want to beat a dead horse with this question, but it is something that has really bothered me for a long time that I can’t audit someone else’s internal experience. I can’t fact-check their reporting, so to speak. Are there any signs to look for, signs to look out for?

Henry Shukman: Yeah. Yeah. Okay. Yes. Sorry. I veered off the point in the question, which was about how do you check for—

Tim Ferriss: I think I probably pushed you pretty hard off of the track. You’d think after 850 episodes, I’d be a little more subtle about it, but yeah.

Henry Shukman: [inaudible 00:31:30]. Well, let me just, yeah, try to bring back. Okay. So, what I was going to say is just, there’s so many kinds of meditation and therefore there’s so many kinds of meditation teacher. There are courses now that are pumping out thousands of mindfulness teachers a year. Just in a decade, that’s at least 10,000. What are you supposed to do?

I mean, first of all, there really are different kinds of practice. To have somebody train you in simple mindfulness to de-stress at the end of the day, or once a week, or something, or at the end of a yoga class, whatever, that’s not high stakes, really. And probably lots of people could learn to do that.

But if it’s a deep guide into existential examination of what it is to be alive, I think we’ve got to be more careful with who we go with. Now, there is no easy answer to this, because I could say like, it’s better if they’ve got some tradition behind them that they’ve been trained in, that’s proven over millennia to have some sort of track record in this.

But then again, there’s all kinds of hazards with lineage, and priestly priesthoods, and inherited power, spiritual authority. It’s not a simple thing. So, what I tend to feel is, that if you can find, again, knowing what you’re looking for. If you’re looking for the sort of deep, deeper side of meditative examination, the ideal, I think, is one where this is what I would do is like, don’t be too hasty in joining something. You know what I mean?

If what you really want is a way of examining your own life and examining your sense of self or something, for example. You want to practice that will do that, and have some track record of doing it. But you don’t want to be somebody saying, “Well, you can’t do that with me unless you join our community,” or something like that. Because why? Why shouldn’t you be able to just do it as the person that you are? You know what I mean?

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, I do.

Henry Shukman: I mean, that’s one thing. Another thing is just the dynamics in a group. They can get so unhealthy so easily, and that can happen in any group. I worked for a company that at one time that had its leadership was kind of a cult-like around one very charismatic boss. So it can happen in any context, but it’s sort of particularly kind of likely or risky or sort of yucky if it happens in a spiritual context. And you can see why it easily might do because the stakes can be presented as so high in spirituality. We’re going to help you with your whole life. And you know what I mean? See what I mean? It can be high stakes.

Midroll 2

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, sure. I think it can be high stakes. I also think that on one hand, you don’t want to be forced into joining a community, but if you’re this itinerant traveler who’s dabbling, dipping their toe into 20 different approaches, it doesn’t always add up to something useful.

Henry Shukman: Well, that’s true. Yeah, but I mean, I would say you shouldn’t have to join a community just to do a practice more deeply. And I mean, to be honest, that’s what attracted me to the Zen that I wound up in, is that there really wasn’t anything to join. They met once a week for two hours and four times a year they did a five-day retreat. But there was no residential community. They were themselves—I’m talking about that center in Oxford, they were themselves part of a network. So they weren’t their own bosses quite, so to speak. They were answerable and accountable to others.

They had a pretty good system of peer relationships among teachers so that teachers weren’t sort of lone wolves who could go off the rails very easily. And there was overall, I think we’re already getting a bit wiser about it in the West compared to 75 years ago when a guru could come in from India and immediately get a sort of following and they become a cult or rather cult-like anyway. But now we know there’s enough practice going on now. There’s enough experience of it in the West for it to start developing more normal approaches really. And for it to be less exotic and less fringe and less weird.

Therefore, we’re asking of it the kind of reasonable requests for norms of organizational savviness or just good sense. See what I mean? In the old days it was, meaning 50 years ago or something, it was still a bit weird. And so if somebody says, “Well, I’m enlightened, come and join my—we’ve got this fantastic residential community, come and join us.” How would you know whether—

Tim Ferriss: I mean, if someone comes up to me and says that now, I would still be pretty skeptical.

Henry Shukman: But then there weren’t that many alternatives perhaps. And people though you had to do it that way. They didn’t know.

Tim Ferriss: Let’s talk about your personal practice and teaching of Zen. It seems like it’s changed in some ways since we last did a podcast together, 2021.

Henry Shukman: Yeah, it’s true. Yeah.

Tim Ferriss: Do you want to describe what the catalysts were and what the outcomes were?

Henry Shukman: Yeah. Well, actually I had a brain injury. I fell off my bike, hit my head and had a pretty mild concussion that had a very long tail, which I’m still not entirely over actually. I’m pretty functional, but stamina’s significantly less. But with that injury, I couldn’t do the kind of, actually the very thing we’re talking about, the dokusan teaching. I would just get completely sort of befuddled and confused.

Tim Ferriss: Dokusan meaning a student would come into you for a one-on-one meeting to discuss their practice.

Henry Shukman: Yes, exactly. Precisely. But there’d be like, could be 20 students.

Tim Ferriss: They’d just be stacked. It’d be open hours.

Henry Shukman: Exactly.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah. Office hours with 20 people in a row.

Henry Shukman: It’s that sort of thing. And in the olden days, I mean, prior to this injury, when I’d be leading a Zen retreat, I might literally in the course of a week do 150 plus dokusans. And that was the way it worked. So I just couldn’t do that. And it was also COVID time. And what I ended up doing was, it’s a bit of a weird story, but just before this injury, I’d been staying in a cabin up in the mountains in Northern New Mexico where I was going to go and rest and just hike and have oatmeal and coffee and a sandwich and just wander around and just chill out. But actually the very first morning as I was making said oatmeal—

Tim Ferriss: You’re like, I hate oatmeal. Can’t do it. No, I’m kidding.

Henry Shukman: While I was making it, I had a sentence came to me and I wrote it down and I ended up writing nonstop for 12 days in yellow pads. And I wrote what became my most recent book actually, Original Love it’s called, which parses out practice into different sort of dimensions, four main areas. And I realized that those four main areas of practice were what I’d been conveying to people individually in Dokusan, depending on what they were concerned with. And so when I could no longer do the practice interviews, I started doing courses that worked through these four areas of practice.

And those were weirdly way more popular than the old hardcore Zen retreats. It was COVID time again, so people could do it in their living room and all that. And it was actually – I’d say it was sort of a, somehow I feel as a more sort of compassionate way of sharing the practice because there’s a tendency in some forms of Zen to be sort of, you’ve got to have this experience. You got to awaken. Awaken man, wake up. That’s what it’s for. And nobody can make that happen. No teacher and no student can force it. It just happens when it happens.

So this other way of teaching was much more sort of open around it all. There’s lots of good stuff you can do that’s not awakening. Awakening is not the only thing. There’s all this other good growth and development and examination you can do that we would not call awakening. So that’s what I was sort of sharing, a more broad approach and a gentler approach actually.

And because of that actually, because I had that structure, when our mutual friend Kevin suggested making an app, I mean this is a bit of the natural, the sort of history of the app actually. I realized that I had this sort of, I don’t know exactly curriculum, but had this framework, these four different sort of faces or dimensions of practice that I’d written a book about and I was giving courses on. But in an app, I could actually help someone go experientially through them. Actually experience these different dimensions of practice, not just read about them.

Henry Shukman: That’s right. The poem becomes like a screen that you’re looking through and you’re seeing something that the poet has been seeing.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, and I’ve seen this now dozens of times. It’s like people who are devout, what would I call them, militant nonfiction readers who are just like—fiction is anathema to them, including poetry. They’re just like, “Why would I waste my time,” basically. And if they have not necessarily just drug facilitated experiences, but certain—I mean, there are lots of different types of experiences, your experience that you had spontaneously, and then suddenly you have this direct experience that allows you to look through that screen.

Henry Shukman: Yeah, exactly.

Tim Ferriss: As opposed to looking at a wall of words and saying, “This doesn’t make any sense.”

Henry Shukman: Yes. I mean, one point I might make on the same topic is just how valuable meditation can be in combination with psychedelics as the very follow-up path. I’ve got friends who have committed psychonauts, and some have found meditation as the thread that will keep alive in some way what they’ve experienced, or at least is a real serious deep response to what’s opened up in them through a psychedelic journey.

And others actually don’t do it. They just want another trip because it feels so good and I don’t want this thing in me to close. But actually meditation is the perfect, I don’t know, antidote to the impulse to just do it again, because it gives you that thread.

Tim Ferriss: I mean, I’ve taken my foot off the gas personally in a really significant way in the last three to five years. With respect to psychedelics, I still think they have a place, but I think they’re overused and I think they’re very well suited to acting as catalysts, not constant interventions necessarily.

Look, if you’re a full-time clinician and you’re practicing in a lineage and let’s say down South, there are some people who are effectively sitting five nights a week. If that is their full-time path that point forward, fine. But otherwise, it generally makes very little sense and you’re probably going to end up in a padded room. There is a survivorship bias with that stuff.

Henry Shukman: Tim?

Tim Ferriss: Yeah.

Henry Shukman: I want to throw in something actually.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, throw away.

Henry Shukman: Let me just see if this fits for you. But the thing you said about the person who was on their phone or having a conversation, I’ve been too busy with non-duality to apply for a job or whatever it was. I mean, I just thought that actually, I mean, it’s hilarious, but a counter example of that is actually my own Zen master, Yamada-san, Yamada Roshi, who has had jobs, very, very demanding jobs for whatever, entire working life and has been deep in Zen practice, which is thoroughly non-dual.

And people often ask him, “How do you balance your Zen with your work life?” And his response is, “There’s nothing to balance. It’s all one thing. The idea that my Zen is separate from my work life is nonsense. It’s like whatever I found in Zen is showing up as work when I’m in the office. It’s showing up sitting when I’m in the Zen dome.” So actually, there really isn’t any kind of dichotomy. I’m really, in a way, if you think there is, you still haven’t got non-dual. The whole point is it’s not two things. You see what I mean?

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, I do.

Henry Shukman: So the non-dual itself has to be almost folded back into ordinary life.

Tim Ferriss: So let’s bat this around a little bit. This is a phone to bat around. So I agree with you that they don’t need to be mutually exclusive. They don’t need to cancel each other out in some way. At the same time, and I have to lean on the psychedelic stuff because I just have so much more context and mileage there than I do with meditation. Even though I’m meditating twice a day, I think that’s probably more than the average bear, but whether I’m being maximally productive in those or not is a separate question.

But the—you haunt my dreams, Henry. In any case, the point I was trying to make is that I agree they don’t need to be mutually exclusive. However, I am curious—let me explain a phenomenon and then I’d be curious if this happens in meditation because I feel like I have seen it in some meditators. All right, somebody has their very demanding job. They work long hours, but they’re putting points on the scoreboard, doing really well, providing for the family, all the things, whatever the specifics happen to be.

Then they have a large reality bending psychedelic experience. Now, you could replace that with meditation retreat and then a bunch of meditation, but I’ll use the psychedelics. And they realize this is just a big fucking game. This is not as life or death or as serious or as necessary as I thought it was. Okay, let’s say that’s Saturday. What do you do Monday morning? So yes, you can go back into playing your game, but the nature, the perspective with which you now play that game is quite different. Do you know what I mean?

Henry Shukman: Yes.

Tim Ferriss: And for some people they’re like—they don’t want to do it anymore or they cut back really dramatically. And so I’m curious with someone like Yamada Roshi, I guess I’m asking you to speak for him on some level, maybe he’s told you. It’s like, okay, so he’s working for some huge bank, working with all these things, and it’s like, eh, how does someone like that—

Or you could speak to the broader phenomenon, it doesn’t have to be limited to Yamada Roshi, but I guess maintain the belief that it is important enough to continue putting the amount of time that I imagine he puts into running or building a business or a division at one point with 3,000, not direct reports, but people under him in the company hierarchy or whatever it might be. Do you see what I’m grasping for here?

Henry Shukman: Yeah, I do. I do.

Tim Ferriss: Because I do, and I don’t view that as losing your edge in a harmful way, but there have definitely been times when I’m just kind of like, what is it? Berchand Russell who said something along the lines of a clear sign of an impending nervous breakdown is taking one’s work incredibly seriously or something like believing your work is incredibly serious. This is something that I have personally struggled with at points.

Henry Shukman: Yeah. I mean—

Tim Ferriss: I’m just like, you’re talking about Oxford and the ephemerality of things and A. E. Housman and you mentioned Oxford. I remember in Oxford going to an exhibit. Oh, I wish I could remember exactly the name of the exhibit, but what matters is I saw a handwritten draft by Percy Shelley, I think it was, of Ozyman—

Henry Shukman: Percy Bysshe of Ozymandias.

Tim Ferriss: —of Ozymandias, which is a great companion too.

Henry Shukman: It is. Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!

Tim Ferriss: I mean, it’s so good. It’s like we can’t even remember the full name of Alexander the Great. Come on. When people are like, “What’s your legacy with your startup?” And I’m like, “Are you fucking kidding me?” There’s part of me that’s just like, “Come on now.” I don’t want to rain on anyone’s parade, but I’m like—

Henry Shukman: Okay, look, let me see if I can—

Tim Ferriss: I realize that was a lot of brain vomit.

Henry Shukman: No, no, it’s excellent.

Tim Ferriss: But they’re not mutually exclusive, but we’re all playing all sorts of games and it’s nice to see the games we’re playing so we’re not unwitting participants in some theater. And at the same time, how do you go in and sell your insurance on Monday morning if you have your awakening experience or get blasted into stardust by some psychedelic?

Henry Shukman: Yeah. Well, look, it’s probably rather a complex field, but let me see what I can do.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, I mean, that was the most incoherent non-question I’ve “asked” in this conversation. Yeah, which is saying something.

Henry Shukman: No, I think it’s a fantastically important, beautiful question, but I don’t know how clear an answer I can give, but let me just see. I mean, the basic point is that as we’re sitting here doing what we’re doing right now, I’m deeply grateful. I’m really enjoying our conversation.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, me too.

Henry Shukman: I’m really grateful that we’re here doing it. There’s a table, carpet, floors.

Tim Ferriss: There’s a table. Least I could do for you, Henry.

Henry Shukman: And a room. I mean, this is here going on and we’re having this conversation. It’ll hopefully go out on your podcast. And all of it is made of the same emptiness, shunyata, as absolutely everything is made of. Now, if you get to see that clearly, and I would say the meditative path to discovering that is a very good one because it happens over time. It’s not a sudden six-hour thing, and you’re sort of rocketed up and you see it or down and you see it and then you’re back. That’s a very difficult way of getting it and then how earth do you integrate it and it’s so on. But on the meditative path, it’s gradual.

Tim Ferriss: Mm-hmm. Now, can I add one sidebar?

Henry Shukman: Yeah.

Tim Ferriss: We talked about it in our first conversation and we’ve talked about it since. You’re not necessarily opposed to psychedelics.

Henry Shukman: No, I’m not. I mean, actually I have—

Tim Ferriss: You have some experience?

Henry Shukman: I had a little bit in the course of my life and recently I’ve had more because I was curious about them. So I tried 5-MeO-DMT and I went to—

Tim Ferriss: Starting with a light lift. Yeah.

Henry Shukman: —but honestly, I went to this extremely familiar place, which is basically what it was for me anyway, was there’s just nothing. There’s this beautiful place of absolutely nothing. And in that place of just nothing, then feeling a lot of love. And it gradually, I came back 20 minutes later or whatever it was. And it was very, very beautiful, but not unfamiliar. And so it wasn’t revelatory. But wait, coming back to the—sorry. So yeah, no, I think—

Tim Ferriss: I just didn’t want people to think this is meditation versus psychedelics like manomaya.

Henry Shukman:

items.title: How propagandists weaponize archaeology to rewrite the past
items.summary: The historian Eric Hobsbawm once said, “Historians are to nationalism what poppy-growers … are to heroin-addicts. [They] supply the essential raw material.” The same holds true for archaeologists. The heritage archaeologists reveal helps groups of people forge collective…
items.author: Sam Kean
items.contentHtml:
The historian Eric Hobsbawm once said, “Historians are to nationalism what poppy-growers … are to heroin-addicts. [They] supply the essential raw material.” The same holds true for archaeologists. The heritage archaeologists reveal helps groups of people forge collective identities and anchor our fleeting lives in something enduring. Spectacular discoveries — King Tut’s mask, the bronzes of Benin, Irish harps — also become national icons and rallying points.

Regrettably, people with political agendas know this and often treat the past as ready-made propaganda — a bin to root through for “evidence” that justifies their goals. And if they can’t find what they need, they have no compunctions about twisting archaeology to suit their purposes.

Consider the Peking Man fossils from China. Despite the singular name, these fossils consist of 40-odd men, women, and children unearthed 30 miles from Beijing starting in 1929. They belong to a hominin subspecies called Homo erectus pekinensis and lived 410,000 to 780,000 years ago.

It’s unlikely that Peking Man was a direct ancestor of modern humans. Homo sapiens originated in Africa 300,000 years ago, then spread globally. Along the way, we interbred in Asia with two other hominins (Neanderthals and Denisovans), so there’s a chance we interbred in China with later ancestors of Peking Man, but most scientists don’t think so. Regardless, archaeologists unanimously trace humankind’s ultimate ancestry to Africa.

Unanimous outside China, at least. Again, humankind does have a modest amount of non-African ancestry — a few percentage points — but ideologues within China push the notion of non-African ancestors way too far. They insist that Peking Man was the very wellspring of humanity.

Sometimes this manifests itself in harmless ways. Before the 2008 Olympics in Beijing, Chinese officials lit the ceremonial relay torch at the quarry where the fossils first turned up. But other beliefs about Peking Man have a sinister edge. In 2012, China’s top propaganda minister published a paper noting that certain traits separate humans from apes — hairless bodies, an upright gait, long legs relative to our arms. He then asserted, with zero evidence, that everyone “knows” Chinese people have the least body hair, the flattest butts when standing, and the shortest arms of any race. The Chinese must “therefore” have evolved into humans first and are farthest along the evolutionary road to perfection.

Sadly, Chinese archaeologists who challenge such claims have been smeared as traitors and “scum.” Worse, opposition to African origins often deteriorates into abuse of African people. As one critic commented, in China, “the most fundamental of scientific questions — where we come from — has been subordinated to the demands of nation, pride, and self-image.”

Archaeology has been dragged into the dispute over Taiwan, as well. In 2024, the Keqiutou Archaeological Museum opened in Pingtan, an island off mainland China that practically stares Taiwan in the face. The museum proposes a radical reinterpretation of Taiwanese history.

Since the 1980s, archaeologists have known that Taiwan’s indigenous, non-Chinese peoples began making excursions to islands in the Pacific Ocean starting 5,000 years ago. Those pioneers eventually settled greater Polynesia. Linguistic, artifactual, and genetic evidence supports this, further demonstrating that Taiwan had a thriving, pre-Chinese culture.

In contrast, the Keqiutou museum argues that Taiwan lacked culture until mainland Chinese people moved to Taiwan 6,500 years ago. It also claims that it was those ethnic Chinese who colonized Polynesia. Curators base this claim on supposed similarities between ancient pottery at different sites and the carbon dating of rice and millet — connections that the vast majority of archaeologists find specious.

Nevertheless, such claims allow the Chinese government to insist that indigenous Taiwanese culture is “really” Chinese deep down, and that Taiwan should therefore belong to mainland China today. Chinese president Xi Jinping himself has alluded to these claims in speeches.

China’s neighbor India also uses archaeology to push nationalistic agendas.

To simplify somewhat, there’s a divide in Indian history between Dravidians and Aryans. (In this context, Aryans are not Caucasians, but an ancient cultural group.) Nowadays, the descendants of Aryans predominate in northern India, while Dravidians inhabit the south. But that tidy split masks a long, fraught relationship.

The standard view of Indian history holds that Dravidians once ranged across all India, north and south. Then, roughly 4,000 years ago, Aryan males began migrating into India from western Asia. The details are murky, but these men probably arrived in waves over several centuries and imported both their language (which became Sanskrit) and the religious practices that shaped modern Hinduism. During this migration, Dravidians were pushed south, and the proto-Hindu culture of the incoming Aryans eventually dominated the subcontinent.

Still, a key detail of the migration remained unknown. Did Aryans push south peacefully and accumulate power gradually, or storm in and conquer?

In the early 1900s, the conquest theory reigned supreme, to the delight of the Aryans’ descendants. They’d long scorned Dravidians as backward and claimed that their ancestors brought culture to a savage land.

But a big discovery flipped that notion on its head. Between 2600 and 1900 B.C., the so-called Indus Valley Civilization (IVC) thrived in what’s now eastern Pakistan and northwest India. This sophisticated urban culture boasted extensive dams, fairly modern sewage and plumbing, and widespread trade networks. It showed no evidence of despotism or war, and it may have had its own written language.

The IVC then vanished from the historical record, until archaeologists unearthed it in the 1920s. This discovery — a lost civilization! — stunned people across the subcontinent. I cover this incredible tale in more detail, alongside the stories of history’s other great lost treasures in my new book, The Museum of Lost Things (2026). For our sake, the timing of the IVC’s decline — just after Aryans began streaming south — raised questions about whether the migrants destroyed it.

Dravidian activists insisted yes. Suddenly, they could paint Aryans as barbarians who swept in and crushed a sophisticated, peace-loving culture. Dravidians had long felt like second-class citizens in India, and they delighted in knocking Aryans down several pegs.

However, later excavations undermined the idea of an invasion. As we now know, rather than collapsing around 1900 B.C., most IVC cities declined gradually as people migrated to smaller settlements, perhaps due to climate change or natural disasters. In sum, the Indus culture didn’t collapse so much as spread out and transform.

This new evidence delighted modern Hindu nationalists, many of whom trace their ancestry to the proto-Hindu Aryans who migrated south. They suddenly felt absolved of blame for the IVC’s decline.

Then they pushed things further. These nationalists desperately want to link Hinduism to the glorious IVC, and they claim to have found proof in the most enigmatic artifacts of the Indus era: tiny stone seals carved with runes.

Linguists today debate whether these runes constitute a true written language. If so, no one has deciphered it. If you squint, however, the strokes and squiggles on the seals resemble early Sanskrit (or so Hindu nationalists claim). To them, this proves that their ancestors never migrated to India but had always been there — and had probably built the IVC. The fact that certain seals showed pictures of people in Hindu yogic poses bolstered their case.

To be clear, the claim that the ancient Aryans founded the IVC is false: both genetic and artifactual evidence show that the Aryans arrived in India after the IVC’s golden age. Furthermore, ancient Sanskrit texts describe a pastoral existence — nothing like urban Indus life. These texts also mention horses, chariots, and armor, none of which appear at IVC sites. The scholarly consensus on all of this is strong.

But that hasn’t stopped Hindu nationalists from arguing otherwise, and the debate has spilled into the wider culture. A 2016 Bollywood epic called Mohenjo Daro (the name of a major IVC site) showed Indus-era people speaking a Sanskritized tongue, despite zero evidence for that possibility. Dravidian activists denounced the film as propaganda. The two sides have also sparred over how the IVC is presented in textbooks, even as far afield as California.

These aren’t just academic debates, either. Nationalists essentially use archaeology as a title deed — arguing that proto-Hindu people have dominated India since the 2000s B.C. and therefore deserve to rule today. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing supporters also glorify the Indus Valley Civilization and use its supposed Hindu roots to justify their policies. It’s Make India Great Again.

Frustratingly for archaeologists, these battles distract from the larger truth: that both Dravidians and Aryans contributed mightily to Indian culture. Certain aspects of modern Hinduism did migrate south with the Aryans, while others were already present among the Dravidians whose ancestors likely populated the IVC. These two cultures then flowed together like two great rivers, and modern India emerged from their union. But amid a culture war, neither side wants to hear that.

To be sure, neither India nor China invented archaeological propaganda.

Nazi Germany used archaeology to justify war crimes. In the 1930s, crooked scholars scoured museums and digs across Europe for artifacts from ancient Germanic tribes. If they could trace any object, however tenuously, to foreign lands like Poland or Czechoslovakia, they trumpeted this as “proof” that ancient Germans once owned those lands, and that modern Poles or Czechs were squatters. The Nazis then felt justified in goose-stepping in and seizing more Lebensraum.

The United States did something similar in the 1800s. One justification for seizing Native American land was that Native Americans had never “done anything” with their vast continent — never built empires with cities and monumental structures.

Except, as early American explorers pushed west, they found exactly such structures: terraced hills, geometric earthworks, and especially giant mounds. Some of these mounds were tombs, while others were temples with roads winding up to the top. There were thousands of mounds overall, some of which stretched nearly as tall as the pyramids of Egypt. At its peak around 1200 A.D., the mound site of Cahokia in Illinois might have had a larger population than London.

But when confronted with this evidence — of a sophisticated culture that pre-dated European contact — U.S. explorers and statesmen didn’t revise their dim views of Native Americans. They simply invented a new theory: that a “lost race” had constructed the mounds instead.

As for who this lost race of mound-builders was, there was no shortage of guesses: Chinese or Polynesian explorers; ancient Egyptians or Hindus; refugees from Atlantis or the Lost Tribes of Israel from the Bible. The most popular theory held that the mound-builders were ancient Europeans, probably Vikings. But any race would do, as long as it wasn’t Native Americans.

Now, a few dissenting scholars raised some inconvenient points here. When Christopher Columbus and other explorers began arriving in the Americas, they found plenty of Native Americans, but zero Chinese, Hebrew, or European people. So if those races built the mounds, where did they go?

Lost race proponents had some ideas. Perhaps hordes of Native Americans had swept in from Asia and wiped the mound-builders out. Others advanced a eugenics-like argument that “degenerate” Native Americans arrived and intermarried with the noble mound-builders, diluting their genetic stock and sapping their vitality.

Regardless, many Americans — especially those who believed that the lost race was European — used this theory to justify genocide. According to them, if Native Americans had exterminated a lost white race once, that now gave white Americans the right to exterminate Native Americans in turn.

This notion of a lost race of mound-builders wasn’t some fringe idea. Noah Webster and Benjamin Franklin supported it, as did presidents William Henry Harrison and Andrew Jackson. Jackson even mentioned the mound-builders in a State of the Union address. He also referenced the lost race of Europeans when justifying the Trail of Tears — the mass deportation of 100,000 Native Americans from the East Coast. One historian called the lost race theory the “governing myth” of the United States in the 1800s.

For better or worse, archaeology unifies countries and peoples every bit as firmly as flags, battles, and epic poems. And with all due respect to Eric Hobsbawm, it’s not always a matter of simply providing “raw material.” Archaeological data often needs interpretation, which leaves it open to manipulation. At that point, archaeology becomes politics by other means.

This article How propagandists weaponize archaeology to rewrite the past is featured on Big Think.

Carlo Rovelli thinks the search for an "ultimate reality" is a mistake, and that physics, Buddhist philosophy, and Wittgenstein all point the same way. Jonny Thomson asks him what's left once you give up on foundations.

On the equality of all things: Carlo Rovelli in conversation with Jonny Thomson

The equality of all things

Jonny Thomson: Hello, everybody, and welcome to today's live conversation. And I'm very excited about this one because I'm speaking to somebody who I've long admired, long adored, actually. And it is Carlo Rovelli, who is a theoretical physicist, who is one of the founders of loop quantum gravity. He's the best-selling author of a series of books such as Seven Brief Lessons on Physics, The Order of Time, and his most recent book is this one here, and it's called On the Equality of All Things, and it brings physics and philosophy together beautifully. So thank you for coming on and agreeing to talk with me today, Carlo.

Carlo Rovelli: Thank you very much for having me. It's a pleasure. It's an honor.

Jonny Thomson: I'm sorry to be boring, but it's the title. I want to talk about the title, On the Equality of All Things. And you start in the preface by saying it comes from a book by Zhuangzi, who is a Taoist philosopher. And it alludes to the anti-foundationalism to which I believe modern science leads us. Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another. Now, some people might find that a bit hard to swallow. What do you mean by that? How is it true that judgments and galaxies and atoms and stones don't differ from each other?

Carlo Rovelli: Well, first of all, you have summarized the book already, and the title is the best part of the book, I think, the title. Well, of course. They differ. They differ in something. Like you and I differ. And I'm different from a cop. What I'm saying there is that we tend to make big, to cut the world in big metaphysical differences, the body and the soul, the abstract things, the concrete things, the natural thing and the artificial human things. And it seems to me that one of the main messages of science is that these are bad divisions, the bad separations. And the more we learn, the more we realize. That the whole varieties of same kind of things. We shouldn't separate the world in kingdoms, totally different areas. That's equality for things.

A monism without a foundation

Jonny Thomson: Is it a kind of monism? So when we talk about monism, for those who don't know, I often instantly think of Spinoza. Spinoza, who is a philosopher who's known for this idea that essentially everything that we see, interact with, including ourselves, are essentially modes of this monosubstance. I often describe it like waves in an ocean, kind of like popping up and going down. Are you a monist in the Spinozian sense then?

Carlo Rovelli: Absolutely, yes. And it is a monism. In fact, it's a reaction against dualism. Reaction because I think that's where modern science is pushing us toward more and more. So I don't, I'm not arguing that I have a rigorous argument for this thesis, but I'm arguing that as far as we know, that's the best way for understanding the world we have. And Spinoza has always been a main inspiration for me. So certainly there is the same kind of monism than in Spinoza, but there is a huge difference. Because Spinoza is a foundationalist, it's a quintessential foundationalist. Namely the variety of aspects of reality, the myriad things, as the Chinese put it, the whole manifestation of one thing, one basic thing.

And many monisms, plural, are efforts to reduce the complexity to one basic thing. Everything is atoms. Everything is physics. Everything is perceptions. Everything is God. Everything is social construction. What I'm reacting to, and that's anti-foundationalism in the sentence that you read, is that this monism doesn't need, I don't think we need that. In fact, I think that's a bad idea to ask what is the basic thing out of which the other derive. Because if we do that, we always put ourselves in trouble. And because it has never worked, nobody has ever convinced anybody. So that's the starting point and everything derives from that. So if we accept complexity, if we accept the richness of reality, if we accept circularity, perspectivalism, we can keep everything together without having to say which one is fundamental.

The atomist dream and its limits

Jonny Thomson: So before I opened the book, I didn't know about the Taoist connection. I actually thought, perhaps it's because I'm reading too much Epicureanism at the moment and Lucretius. I thought it was a nod to On the Nature of Things, which is this great poem by Lucretius. So are you saying you disagree with the fundamental Greek ambition to find the, because atom means literally indivisible, the least, the smallest possible building block of the universe. Do you disagree with that kind of Greek effort to find?

Carlo Rovelli: You're really putting myself in trouble here because the answer is yes. And I say this with sorrow in my heart because. Spinoza is my master and Lucretius is my even greater master. I mean, the inspiration of my life and ancient atomism, Democritus and Epicurus, Lucretius. These are marvelous teachers for all of us. They certainly pushed out to understand the unity of all things. In fact, if I can go back one second, what is marvelous in Spinoza is that it's a unity of all things which are the substance of everything, but also God and also the reality, the material reality, nature, but also the emotions and also our reason. It's just part of the same story. Now, Democritus and Lucretius tell us this great story on which physics, my trade, has been inspired so strongly. I mean, Newton was certainly great inspiration there, found great inspiration there, that we can understand everything that the words that Democritus used just in terms of the void and atoms.

And Lucretius is marvelously telling this grand story. The entire nature of everything can be understood just in terms of world of atoms and the void. To some extent, it's a dream of theoretical physics. physicalist, I do think that every phenomenon is a physical phenomenon. Or more precisely, every time two phenomena differ, there is something physically different in the two cases. To make the point, I think you went through one of your previous conversations. If there's a situation in which I have in my mind a goblin doing something and another situation is everything the same, but I don't have in my mind that image. Necessarily, there is something different physically in my mind. So there cannot be somebody thinking about a fantastic creature without something in the mind of this person being physically different. From the case in which you wouldn't.

So I think everything is physics in that sense. But the dream in Democritus, and that's bad, I was getting at, that if we get the atoms, we understand everything. And it's also the dream in Lucretius, right? Once we understand that everything atoms, everything flows and follow, It's also the dream of enlightenment. If enough clarity, enough reason, we clarify everything. I think it's over. So he said to his after the... enlightenment because the world is too complex and understanding basic physical rules does not mean understanding reality and its complexity. In fact, understanding reality means understanding the complexity quite a lot respectively of the independent physics.

If I ride a bicycle which is in plastic and ride a bicycle which is in iron, the physics of the two bicycles is totally different, profoundly different, but it's the same bicycle. So it's more relevant for me to think of the bicycle in terms of bicycle notions. Or as I sometimes put it, if my bicycle breaks, I don't take it to a particle physicist at CERN because he knows the standard model of neutrons, electrons and protons to fix it. I take it to the mechanics. And that does not mean that I don't think that my bicycle is just protons, electrons and neutrons.

Of course it is. But that's completely relevant for the understanding of the bicycle. So in that sense, I'm not a... My monism, the monism that I think we're pushed toward by science, is not this one fundamental level everything follows. There are many levels, they're coherent. And there isn't, we don't have to look for one for justifying the others.

There is no hard problem of consciousness

Jonny Thomson: That's very interesting. Thank you. I should say for those listening who hadn't heard the interview that you had mentioned there, I was talking at the time about what people in the philosophy of mind call qualia, which is this idea of experience. And there is a big debate in the philosophy of mind, which is that saying that, you know, experience and that feeling of subjective first personhood is very hard to square in a physicalist model, as you seem to have been laying out there. So as I understand it, you think that the hard problem of consciousness, which says that we will never really ever get to grips with this idea of experience and subjectivity.

Is nonsense. Actually, you think there is no hard problem of consciousness. Can you explain why you think that is?

Carlo Rovelli: Yeah, I think that the hard problem of consciousness is nonsense. A number of reasons. First of all, the expression hard problem of consciousness comes from David Chalmers. And if you look at the way he put it precisely, he says, imagine that we have understood everything we can understand scientifically or with observation about the brain and blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Imagine all that. Well, we will still have a problem. And that seems to me a nonsensical statement, because how can I imagine to know what I don't know? OK, it's just you're imagining with what you know, and you're just patching together things that you know and putting in different manners.

It's a fact that we know so little about the way our brain works. If I argued, imagine, I mean, thunderstorms are not well understood yet. Thunderstorm is a very complicated thing. And I imagine that, you know, you know everything physical to know about thunderstorm, but still thunderstorm is not, you don't get it. It's a nonsensical, you know, when we have understood it, we will think if we have understood them or not. To argue a priori. That something is inconceivable is to misunderstand what learning means. Learning doesn't mean adding new pieces of bits of information about reality. It means changing our way of thinking. When we learn relativity, Newton theory, Maxwell theory, We didn't just add something to the previous knowledge. We changed the way we were thinking. Maxwell changed the Newtonian way about things. Before Newton, the bodies and forces are distance. Maxwell introduces a field in between. It's a new way of thinking.

Things that seemed incomprehensible before become comprehensible, etc. When we understand better what Chalmers calls the easy problem of consciousness, which is not easy at all, it's just to understand what happened in mammals and in us. we'll be able to see whether there is more to understand or not. But that's a sort of a preliminary side remark. The key point is that I think there is an assumption here, which is that science is about, you know, how things move, a little both attacking each other mechanism, understanding the mechanism. But science is not that. That's the science of the 19th century, or maybe the 18th century, already with the late 19th century changed. If you look at quantum mechanics, Quantum mechanics, it doesn't say how things happen. It's a theory about how things influence other things.

So science is about how things manifest themselves to one another. So the main argument, which is often done by people by Nagel, or Chalmers, that the first person perspective, it's unreachable for science because science is always a third person perspective, is wrong because science is always in a first person perspective, never in a third person perspective. The idea that science is a description of the world from the outside, from the eyes of God, is an 18th century idea. It's not science of today. Science of today is the day that we describe the world from within.

All description are from a perspective. So we understand things in terms of their manifestation, their phenomena. So phenomena are not mysterious, are the thing we're talking about. The entire debate about qualia, subjectivity, I think is grounded on a misunderstanding of what science is.

Will science ever hit a ceiling?

Jonny Thomson: It's interesting because the more you talk, the more I wonder about whether this applies to the science more broadly. And, you know, it's a problem which goes all the way back to Plato and the Meno dialogue about, you know, the idea of that. How can we know what to look for if we don't know what to look for? And we are constantly limited by our first personhood and our subjectivity. Does that mean that science will have a hard ceiling, at which point we can no longer go beyond our expectations, our concepts and the way that we slice and dice the world is always going to be limited to our human minds.

And so therefore, science will eventually cap out at some point. I mean, what the pragmatists argued that science would eventually reach a point of we can go no further. This is all humans agree that this is the best science available. Do you think that that's true?

Carlo Rovelli: No, because that presupposes that there is this wall a priori there, and there is a final thing to be reached which is unreachable. But there's a fantasy of the final thing, which I think is not a good fantasy. We know about the world we know about is what we know about the world. That's the world for us. And we know we can learn more. Of course, we know we can learn more because we've been learning more all our life as individual humans and as civilization. So we expect we'll be learning more. In fact, we do learn more every day, right?

Every day. I open the window, I see whether it's raining or not. I learn something more about reality. Today is not raining. So we constantly learn. So the world is open. And now if somebody has a fantasy that there is an absolute final total reality out there, which is there and it's unreachable for me because I'm limited step by step. I mean, that's not our, that's not the world, that's not us, that's not science. The world is this, let me put it this way. We are part of the world. I'm a physicist, there's no doubt. You and I are just mammals, examples of a phenomenon that happened on this planet, many phenomena that happened in the universe. And yet, this very universe that we describe, we think, It's we think at reality of the world because we have concept, we have way of thinking, we have senses and we make a picture of it. So there is this circularity. The world we're talking about is the world for us. And in that world, we are part of it. Now, this circularity is disturbing if somebody wants, that's anti-foundationalism, if somebody wants to say, okay, okay, but what is the starting point? Starting point is absolute reality there, out of which I came out. No, I cannot get there anymore. The starting point is my perception, okay?

And then I don't understand and how all this world independent from me can exist independent of my perception. So these are bad questions, in my opinion, in the sense in which Wittgenstein has talked us not to ask bad questions, right? There are things we can say about the world, and let's say them. As scientists, as philosophers, as human beings, let's talk about those, not about what is outside our world.

What does it mean to exist?

Jonny Thomson: I'm glad you mentioned Wittgenstein, because at the end of your lessons five, I should say the book is divided into lessons. And then at lesson five, you talk about the notion of existence, what it means to exist as the examples you give of a unicorn, an idea, an atom, a number to exist. And your answer is that you say that we should we should talk in terms of concepts that help us navigate the world. Yeah. Which it sound that sounded to me very pragmatist. Do you identify as being a pragmatist in that sense?

Carlo Rovelli: The problem about identifying being some Easter is that as soon as you do that, people jump on you and say, yes, yes, but the pragmatist also imply that, that, that, that. I don't want that. So I prefer not identifying in any East of any sort. But I c
