items.title: These 5 “what ifs” could have changed cosmic history
items.summary: 13.8 billion years ago, what we know today as our observable Universe began with the most important origin event in cosmic history: the hot Big Bang. Once the Universe became filled with matter, antimatter, and radiation in an almost-perfectly uniform fashion, it expanded and…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
13.8 billion years ago, what we know today as our observable Universe began with the most important origin event in cosmic history: the hot Big Bang. Once the Universe became filled with matter, antimatter, and radiation in an almost-perfectly uniform fashion, it expanded and gravitated in nearly perfect balance. As the Universe cooled, the matter and antimatter annihilated away, leaving a tiny, minuscule, but significant amount of matter behind. After 9.2 billion years, what would become our Solar System gradually began to form from a collapsing cloud of molecular gas, and after another 4.55 billion years or so, humanity first arose on planet Earth.

When we look out at the Universe from our perspective in the here-and-now, we only get a snapshot of all of existence: defined by the properties of the light, particles, and gravitational waves that we observe at the moment of their arrival. Based on all that we’ve seen, combined with our theories, frameworks, and models that reflect the fusion of those observations with the underlying laws of physics, we’ve come to understand the cosmos around us.

However, if things had been only a tiny bit different initially, the outcomes that resulted all throughout our Universe would have been altered dramatically. Here are five things that could have happened, but didn’t, that would have changed the course of our shared cosmic history.

1.) What if the Universe were actually perfectly uniform when it was born?

This one is not something that’s greatly appreciated: the Universe, as we know it, couldn’t have been born perfectly smooth. If we had possessed an exactly equal amount of matter-and-antimatter-and-radiation everywhere, at all locations in space, going all the way back to the earliest moments of the hot Big Bang, every point in the Universe would have experienced an equal gravitational force pulling on it in all directions. The idea of gravitational growth and collapse, which is required to make stars, galaxies, planets, humans, and the grand cosmic web, all relies on a set of initial imperfections to begin growing from.

Without any such seeds, you can’t get the desired end result of structure, including structures such as a star, galaxy, or something even larger. The only hope would then be something that originated from the quantum-scale fluctuations inherent to the nature of the Universe. Because we have quantum processes that cannot be avoided:

  • inherent uncertainties in the positions and momenta of particles,
  • inherent uncertainties between the energy in a system and the amount of time that passes,
  • and exclusion rules that prevent certain particles from occupying identical quantum states,

some amount of imperfections will automatically arise even if there were none initially.

From these quantum processes, you’d expect the initial imperfections that the Universe was born with to arise at around the 1-part-in-10³⁵ level, which is an extremely tiny amount. For comparison, as informed by observations, our Universe was born with imperfections that arose at the 1-part-in-30,000 level. This, too, is small, and means that on average, our actual Universe was born uniform to within 99.997% precision. However, the imperfections that our actual Universe was birthed with are absolutely enormous compared to the tiny quantum fluctuations that arise from the mundane processes that occur today: more than 30 orders of magnitude larger.

Based on the way that imperfections grow in the Universe, it took somewhere around ~100 million years for the largest of the initial fluctuations that the Universe started off with to form the first stars. If the Universe would have been born with fluctuations that were 1-part-in-10,000,000 (ten million) instead, we’d very likely only be forming the first stars now. The reason is simple: gravitational growth takes a very long time unless you start from a substantially large seed, and only once the overdense regions become about twice as dense as the average density does gravitational growth start to meaningfully accelerate.

If our Universe were born exactly, perfectly uniform, then even by today, 13.8 billion years after the Big Bang, there would be no structure, no stars, and no interesting chemical reactions to speak of anywhere in the cosmos.

2.) What if the expansion rate and the effects of gravitation were less perfectly balanced?

This one is a bit tricky. We normally think of the Universe as a fairly stable place, but that’s only because there are two cosmic properties that have been so well-balanced for so long: the rate at which the Universe expands and the decelerating effects of all the matter and radiation in the Universe. Today, these two effects don’t match, and that’s why we say the expansion of the Universe is accelerating. The fact that there’s a third meaningfully energetic component to the Universe, dark energy, is what causes that mismatch, and therefore is what drives the current accelerated expansion of the cosmos.

However, for the first ~6 billion years of the Universe’s history, the expansion rate and the effects of matter-and-radiation didn’t just match, they matched so perfectly well that what we know of as dark energy would have been completely undetectable, even if a hypothetical alien civilization were to develop the exact tools we use today to measure the Universe. The further back in time you go, the less important dark energy becomes relative to matter and radiation. And we can go back not just billions of years, but all the way back to the first tiny fraction-of-a-second after the hot Big Bang.

Here, we can find all the matter and energy we have in the Universe today compressed into a much, much smaller region of space. At this time, the Universe was not only hotter and denser, but expanded much, much more quickly than it’s expanding today. In fact, one way to picture the expanding Universe is to treat it as a race: between the initial expansion rate — whatever that rate was when the hot Big Bang first occurred — and the total effects of all the matter, antimatter, neutrinos, radiation, etc., that are present.

What’s remarkable is when we consider how perfectly balanced these two quantities must have been. Today, the Universe has a density of about 1 proton per cubic meter of space. But early on, it had a density that was more like quintillions of kilograms per cubic centimeter of space. If you would have increased or decreased that density by just 0.00000000001%, the Universe would have:

  • recollapsed on itself, ending in a Big Crunch after less than 1 second, in the case of an increase,
  • or expanded so quickly that no protons and electrons would ever have found one another to form even a single atom in the Universe, in the case of a decrease.

This incredible balance, along with the need for it, highlights just how precarious our existence in this Universe is, and how perfectly in balance the initial expansion rate and the initial matter-and-energy density needed to be.

3.) What if there had been exactly equal amounts of matter and antimatter?

This is another problematic one for us, and in fact it’s one of the greatest unsolved problems in all of physics: why do we live in a Universe with more matter than antimatter? This puzzle has many possible resolutions, but no definitive answer at the present time. What we can say, for certain, is the following:

  • In the early stages of the hot Big Bang, the Universe should have been perfectly symmetric between matter and antimatter, with one equal-and-opposite antimatter particle for every quantum of matter that existed.
  • Somehow, some process occurred that resulted in the creation of an asymmetry where none existed initially, leading to the existence of approximately 1,600,000,001 matter particles for every 1,600,000,000 antimatter particles.
  • Afterward, when the excess of 1,600,000,000 matter particles and 1,600,000,000 antimatter particles annihilated away, we were left with that one extra particle of matter amidst a leftover bath of radiation.

This story repeated itself everywhere over the entire Universe, resulting in about one extra atom per cubic meter of space compared to about a billion photons in that same cubic meter. That radiation still survives, as does the matter, which is why we can reconstruct what happened at early times.

We still don’t know how it happened, but we do know what our Universe would have looked like if we didn’t generate a matter-antimatter asymmetry: the matter and antimatter would have annihilated away, not completely, but until there was so little matter and antimatter left that the individual particles that were left — protons and antiprotons, electrons and positrons, etc. — would simply no longer find each other.

Today’s Universe, you’ll recall, has about ~1 proton per cubic meter of space: if you smeared out the entire Universe and drew a box that was 1 meter × 1 meter × 1 meter, you’d expect to find about 1 proton inside. When you work out the math for what happens if matter and antimatter annihilated away from a perfectly symmetric state, you’d find a very different Universe. Radiation would keep scattering off of these particles for tens of millions of years, rather than just a few hundred thousand, and the average density of all forms of matter and antimatter would be the equivalent of only ~1 proton (or antiproton) per cubic mile: a box that was 1 mile × 1 mile × 1 mile, or about 10 billion times less dense than the Universe we have today.

If our Universe hadn’t created a matter-antimatter asymmetry early on, none of the remarkable steps that came afterward to lead to our existence could have taken place, including the formation of atoms, the formation of stars and galaxies, or the assembly of complex molecules.

4.) What if there hadn’t been any dark matter?

This one is a fascinating possibility to consider that’s generally greatly underappreciated. Most of us think about dark matter as the “glue” that holds the largest structures in the Universe together: things like the cosmic web and enormous galaxy clusters. But dark matter also does two particularly important things we don’t typically think about:

  • It provides the majority of the gravitational mass that both forms all galaxies in the Universe and continues to hold them together.
  • And it prevents structure from being “washed out” by the interactions that exist between normal matter and radiation.

Both of these effects are incredibly important. The large gravitational mass provides a place for normal matter to fall into, the lack of interaction of dark matter with radiation prevents it from being pushed back out, and when stars form, that extra mass prevents stellar winds from expelling the matter.

If you were to take that dark matter away, here’s what would happen instead. The small-scale structure you’d attempt to form wouldn’t exist, as the early radiation-dominated phase of the Universe would wash those imperfections away. Meanwhile, the large-scale galaxies that you did form, requiring more time for gravitational collapse, would undergo one burst of star-formation only, and then those stars would boil all the surrounding matter away, ejecting it from the galaxy entirely. In a Universe with no dark matter, only that first generation of stars would exist, meaning there would be no rocky planets, no biochemistry, and no life around any of them.

5.) What if dark energy weren’t constant in space or time?

This is the one possibility that’s still on the table for our Universe: that dark energy might evolve in some fashion. To the best of our observational limits, it certainly looks and behaves like a cosmological constant — as a form of energy inherent to the fabric of space itself — where the energy density remains constant in time and all throughout space. Although there are some hints, driven by DESI, that dark energy might be weakening, the evidence is flimsier than most people will readily admit.

However, we don’t have constraints on how dark energy behaved (or whether it even existed!) for roughly the first ~50% of our Universe’s history, and we only observe it to be a constant to the limits of our current precision. Four telescopes will improve on this in the very near future: the ESA’s EUCLID, the NSF’s Vera Rubin Observatory, NASA/Caltech’s SPHEREx, and NASA’s Nancy Roman Telescope. Roman, the most precise of them all, should measure whether dark energy changes at all to a precision of just 1%, which will either confirm or rule out the suggested 10% evolution that is consistent with DESI data.

If dark energy strengthens, the Universe could rip apart. If dark energy weakens or reverses its sign, the Universe could yet recollapse. And if dark energy decays, the Universe as we know it could end. None of these things have happened yet, indicating that if dark energy does evolve, its evolution is only very slight, at least so far. It’s possible that any of those evolutions could have taken place in the past, and if dark energy had strengthened or weakened by too much, it would have precluded our existence from occurring at all.

All of this, when taken together, leads us to a fascinating conclusion: if any of these things had been — in any way — substantially different from the way they actually are, it would have been a physical impossibility for human beings to have arisen as we did within the Universe. A Universe that was too smooth would have failed to create stars and galaxies in time; a Universe that expanded too quickly or slowly wouldn’t have remained stable for long enough to form anything interesting. A Universe without more matter than antimatter couldn’t have formed stars, and a Universe without dark matter couldn’t have hung onto their remnants to form planets.

In many ways, we’re extremely fortunate to have gotten the Universe that we occupy, as if any one of a great number of things were even a little bit different, the Universe would not have admitted the existence of humans, or any intelligent observer, as a possibility. But in this cosmos of ours, exactly the way it is, we fully suspect that there are several trillion galaxies present. Around one of the ~400 billion stars in one of them, the Milky Way, life took hold, survived, thrived, and evolved. After more than 4 billion years, human beings arose, and now we look out at the Universe to learn our place in it. It may not have been an inevitable journey from the Big Bang to us, but it sure has been a remarkable one.

This article was first published in May of 2023. It was updated in November of 2026.

items.contentHtml:
Henry Shukman (@henryshukman) is an authorized Zen master in the Sanbo Zen lineage, one of only a few dozen in the world, and spiritual director emeritus of Mountain Cloud Zen Center in Santa Fe, New Mexico. items.title: The deep work routine that changed my life
items.summary: If you can spend 8 hours building someone else’s dream, you can spend 1 hour building your own. But how you use that 1 hour determines everything. If you were to focus on the one thing that leads to the most progress toward your ideal life, for 1 hour a day, first thing in the…
items.author: DAN KOE
items.contentHtml:
If you can spend 8 hours building someone else’s dream, you can spend 1 hour building your own.

But how you use that 1 hour determines everything.

If you were to focus on the one thing that leads to the most progress toward your ideal life, for 1 hour a day, first thing in the morning when your mind is clear and distractions are minimal, for 6-12 months, that’s 365 potential hours invested in the life you want. You can do far more than you think in that amount of time.

For most of my life, I worked 2-4 hours a day.

I feel like influencers flexing their millions put a sour taste in people’s mouth, but for the sake of results, I’ll flex a bit. Those 2-4 hours are exactly how I built an audience that’s closing in on 5 million followers across all platforms, and I’ve made just around $10m from my personal brand alone, not my other companies. That’s the time I used to put out posts, articles, newsletters, YouTube videos and podcasts. That’s also how I wrote 2 books with 2 more on the way - no AI writing involved.

And when I had a 9-5 job, I didn’t have 12 hours a day to make my side business a success. I had 1-2 hours, and a few more on the weekend.

If you want the stupid simple deep work routine, go ahead and skip to the last section of this letter.

But if you have a greater attention span than a goldfish, and understand that the “actionable advice” you crave so bad means nothing without context, I would encourage you to read every section. Bookmark this if you are short on time and set a reminder to come back to it.

You are free to skip to the later sections, but if you have a greater attention span than a goldfish, I would encourage you to read every section. Bookmark this if you are short on time and set a reminder to come back to it.

Let’s discuss why busy people end up on the bottom, why pursuing anything but your life’s work is a waste of time - especially as jobs go extinct slowly then all at once, and finally, how to structure your day not only for maximum productivity, but for maximum leverage.

Enjoy.

I – For most of human history, the busiest people were the lowest status.

Aristotle said we work so that we can have leisure, and that without it no one becomes wise.

Seneca said that the busiest people were often the least accomplished, because they spent their days on everything except their own lives.

Leisure used to be a mark of status while busyness was a mark of obligation. Busyness belonged to slaves, serfs, and laborers who worked from sunrise to sundown.

At some point in the last century, that flipped.

“I’m so busy” became a badge of honor, even when most people knew they were working on nothing meaningful, with nothing to show except time invested in someone else’s vision.

I believe that this flip will happen again.

Soon, it will be seen (more than it already is) as low status to be glued to your computer, sending messages back and forth to Claude all day. We all have big dreams and aspirations, but it requires a certain level of creativity to achieve those dreams without 12 hours of “hard work” as your main strategy.

Time for thinking, strategizing, and creativity will be the mark of high status. In many cases, it will be reserved for the rich.

Now, when I say I worked 2-4 hours a day above, that was somewhat of a lie.

As a writer, if you were to add up the time I spend walking, reading, learning, thinking, and even sleeping... I “work” 24 hours a day. Because all of those activities fuel the quality of my writing, and one hour of writing a day can reach millions of people, and if a fraction of those people purchase from me or my business, I can make millions of dollars. Some people can’t wrap their head around this, because their income is tied to their time spent doing labor. They do not earn from the creative ability of their mind, which will only become more and more of a requirement in the future.

This is mostly why we’re building Eden. It is where you grow your audience and build a digital business. It’s where you sell your products, save all your ideas and bookmarks, and turn those unique ideas into content. If that content gets traction, then you promote your work and get paid for it. There’s a ￼30 day sprint that walks you through all of this. It’s a measly $5.

II - The historical normal is to be self-employed, working a job was a temporary glitch.

Specialization is in fact only a fancy form of slavery wherein the ‘expert’ is fooled into accepting his slavery by making him feel that in return he is in a socially and culturally preferred, ergo, highly secure, lifelong position.

– Buckminster Fuller

During Industrialization, everything became a factory.

Schools included.

The sole purpose of a school system is to prepare children for the jobs of its time, and the jobs at the time were factory jobs - and I can’t help but wonder how education is going to look when the jobs of our time drastically change, or just become meaningless. I believe we are heading into a Second Renaissance, but I’ll save that for later.

Bells marked the start and end of the day. Kids are grouped by age, like batches. Subjects are split up, like an assembly line. Grades and tests were quality checks. Students were rewarded for doing what they were told, on someone else’s schedule, toward someone else’s goal.

Everyone reading this likely went through this system.

And since the mind is shaped through conditioning, and our identity latches onto that which provides us security and comfort, we are all in some way unconsciously tied to a style of work that was only an experiment.

The modern concept of a job is only 100-200 years old. Homo sapiens are 300k years old. Working 9-5, being paid a wage, and having your worth attached to your title is not normal, and it definitely isn’t beneficial to how our brains are wired. Life quickly becomes mechanical.

Work used to mean owning your work.

In 1800, most Americans were farmers, farm workers, or ran a family business. The word “job” meant one piece of work until the late 1700s. It did not mean 40+ years of your life.

The Renaissance ideal was the “universal man” who did many things well. Craftsmen worked under a guild, progressing from apprentice to journeyman to master. “Masterpiece” first meant the work you made to prove you were a master.

I believe history is repeating itself, as it always does, and we are entering the era of the craftsman. A craftsman’s worth was determined by how they used their tools. Today a laptop, the internet, and AI are cheap tools anyone can own. The craft they pursue, their vision for their work, and obsession over the details is what makes the difference. Anyone can build anything, but attention is finite, so only those who treat their work as their life’s work, pouring their heart and soul into what they do will rise above.

In The Third Wave, Alvin Toffler had a similar theory.

He called it the Electronic Cottage, which he saw as the third wave of work.

The first wave was farming, people mostly made what they used. The second wave was the factory, which split people into producers and consumers. The third wave is information and computers, where work moves back home. We once again become creators.

His argument is that a lot of work was “cottage industry,” where families spun, wove, and made goods at home. The factory pulled work out of the home and into one big building. He predicted that computers would reverse that and bring work home again (I’m sitting in my office, in my underwear, at 10:09 am, writing this, by the way).

During the First Wave most people consumed what they themselves produced. They were neither producers nor consumers in the usual sense. They were instead what might be called prosumers.

I believe that’s what a creator is. Not a content creator per se, although social media is where a creator would find their audience in today’s world, until social media is replaced with another form of media.

A friend I have online sells cotton apparel because he is against polyester clothing. I can get my apparel from him. Another online friend teaches philosophy, I can get my education from him. Another sells software. Another sells and ships baked goods. So on and so forth. I can pursue my interests and find a wedge in a digital tribe that I can contribute best to - we call this a “niche.” The creator economy has had its ups and downs, but at the end of the day, I see it as a digital society where we can learn, earn, create, and contribute to each other’s lives. That is the modern renaissance lifestyle.

Marshal McLuhan called this the global village where our specialist and fragmented civilization begins to retribalize.

If you have any desire to pursue your interests, do what you want with your life, and become adaptable enough to not have to worry about job loss:

Subscribe now

III – I’m begging you to go all in on your life’s work

There are almost 7B people on this planet. Someday, I hope, there will be almost 7B companies.

– Naval Ravikant

If you are up to date with tech and AI, you’ve probably heard something like this:

Software is dead. Info is dead. Companies are dead. Everything is dead. Everyone is just going to build their own software and get the information they need with AI.

So what do you do when it feels worthless to even start?

First, everything is not dead. Social media is great at keeping you complacent.

Jake Paul, of all people, has pivoted to the info space - look at his business YouTube channel, because frankly they are still the best way for creators to monetize, even when AI has all information (hint: if someone doesn’t know what to ask AI, and they don’t know what good advice looks like, then they won’t get the information they need - humans will be proxies for education and information for people who resonate with their point of view.)

Second, considering people don’t even cook their own food and pay far too much for Uber Eats, I highly doubt they will build their own software. Building a tool to replace a $10-20 subscription instead of focusing on one lever-moving action that makes $1000 an hour is foolish.

Plus, I would rather pay someone who’s made it their life’s work to create the best, say, content scheduling app than build one myself (although that’s what I built), there aren’t going to be 1000 content schedulers in the future. I would rather pay the craftsman who is going to obsess over the details, because obsessing over the details myself would just distract me from moving my own priorities forward.

“Anyone can build anything” is the greatest distraction of our time when we are all painfully aware that long-term focus on one meaningful goal with high potential payoff is what leads to the greatest result and most fulfillment. The future isn’t everyone building everything, but everyone building their one thing and trading with each other. A global village.

In that case, the best course of action is to discover what your life’s work is, and use the tools available to you to build it and spread it to an audience of people who resonate with your mission.

Your “life’s work” is work that allows you, specifically, to unleash the full creative ability of your mind, so that you have a vessel for your potential and contribute to humanity at your fullest.

It is difficult to label exactly what your life’s work is. It isn’t something you need to name. People get hung up on knowing exactly what they do as their life’s work. This isn’t a job. It’s not a set string of tasks. It’s a path in the unknown. It is a way of life where your learning, thinking, and acting are in harmony, and you are contributing to yourself and the world in a way only you can.

That means the work you choose must be something you have a deep interest in, and allows for near-infinite upward movement.

In other words, you’ll probably have to become an entrepreneur of some form.

Because with a “job,” as we define it today, there tends to be a low skill ceiling. You reach a point where you’ve learned enough to coast, the work becomes repetitive and mundane, and you get bored with no freedom to grow into your next shell, until even that shell becomes too constrained, so you overindulge in degenerative activities.

The question then is:

How do you find the thing that you, specifically, were meant to do?

And how do you turn that into your work so that you can comfortably survive and reap the meaning that comes from impacting others?

IV – One hour a day. One meaningful project. One vision for the future.

Code and media are permissionless leverage. They’re the leverage behind the newly rich. You can create software and media that works for you while you sleep.

– Naval Ravikant (again)

To tie this all together:

  • Non-busyness is the new mark of status, and it is required for true creative thinking

  • The pendulum is swinging back to self-employment and entrepreneurship being the norm, take advantage early

  • If you want to compete, you must pursue your life’s work - you must dedicate yourself to one thing, avoid distractions, not try to build everything, and focus on quality and craftsmanship - or else you will be bucketed in with everyone else producing slop

All of these things are arguing the importance of one thing - leverage.

Leverage is getting more of a result per hour of effort, because something other than your time keeps doing the work after you stop.

Creative thinking, entrepreneurship (freedom of work), and experience are necessary pre-requisites to leverage. It is the only way to compete in a world of ‘everyone can do anything.’ Committing to anything but your life’s work is a death sentence.

At a job, the employee mindset you adopt conditions your mind to be anti-leverage. And most people have this way of thinking deeply ingrained in them.

Most people need to be told what to do. They have difficulty accepting that anything can be figured out through the process of trial and error - that’s how the world as we know it came to be, and people did in fact do incredible things before there were instruction manuals for doing them.

Most people can’t dissociate time from money. They see a task’s worth as flat, because as long as they show up for 40 hours a week, they’ll get a paycheck. They cannot fathom that there is some way to make an entire months worth of their income in an hour, if they simply focused only on the tasks with the highest leverage.

As an example, I can publish an X article, and that article can somehow amass a freakish 260 million views, and 1% of those people visit a product page, and 1% of them purchase that product for $150, that’s $3.9 million.

But those are crazy numbers.

What if you post consistently, to the point of generating a few hundred thousand impressions a month (not that hard to do, if you learn and actually try and don’t quit after 2 weeks - it takes longer than 2 weeks to get good at something silly), and you understand that you can tweak the post, the landing page, and the offer to increase conversions to an “okay” 2.5%, then that’s more money than you’d know what to do with.

That’s leverage.

You have posts that generate traffic, and you have a product that sells while you sleep. Both are in alignment with your life’s work.

It’s like dating. If you (the product) are valuable, but you don’t put yourself in front of men/women (traffic), then you aren’t going to get a date. It’s obvious. If you (the product) aren’t valuable, and you put yourself in front of a ton of men/women (traffic) then you probably won’t get a date either, at least not one that you want.

Outside of finding what your life’s work is, those are quite literally the only things that matter. Improving what you offer - a product or service - and iterating on your posts, ads, sponsorships or whatever else you use to generate traffic. For someone who doesn’t have capital to invest or a proven offer, your best bet is organic posts on social media.

I made this Life’s Work Finder AI that interviews you to find your life’s work, then tells you what your content topics could be, and what first product you could sell, then helps you set it all up in Eden to start posting and selling.

Translating this - what do you actually do?

Block out 1 hour a day.

Work on 1 meaningful project.

Aim for 1 vision for your future.

Take it 1 day at a time, for 1 year.

1 hour of deep work is better than 0 hours, and you can drastically change your life in 365 hours.

Then, increase to 2 hours, maybe even 3. You’ll have other work to do as well, but I’m more worried about focusing on executing the highest priority, highest leverage task first thing in the morning to ensure it gets done.

Because when was the last time you asked yourself, before you started working, if I were to do one thing today, what would take me the furthest to my goal?

Probably never.

So what do you do during that one hour?

If you don’t have a product, build one during that hour.

Once you have the product, start writing content.

That’s how businesses are built right now.

Look at Jordan Peterson, Andrew Huberman, and the rest. They probably don’t register themselves as “content creators” or “personal brands.” They have a deep obsession with their interests, they share their learnings and worldview with the world in hopes of helping people.

They use content as the way to capture attention, because that’s where the attention is right now. It doesn’t matter if you don’t like social media - good luck building a business with the newspaper or radio as your distribution.

I’ll write more on this in future articles.

For now, you can find more of my writing here, use Eden to grow your audience and start an online business here, and use the Life’s Work Finder to implement everything we talked about here.

– Dan

items.title: The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently
items.summary: “There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them…
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.contentHtml:
“There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.”

Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more. (Big Think members can get first access to watch the full video at this link.)

But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day. But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought?

I feel as if it’s my philosophical duty to raise doubts where no doubts existed before. And so, here are five “facts” that are actually far more disputed in life — and on Wikipedia — than you might have thought.

1. The Wright brothers invented the airplane

Of course! If you’re feeling really bookish, you could add “Kitty Hawk, December 1903.” The story of the Wright brothers is such a Hollywood-ready fact that it’s almost impossible to forget: two bicycle makers, one windy beach, and twelve seconds in the air.

Unless you went to school in Brazil. Brazilians have two objections to the Wright brothers’ claim: First, no official watched their 1903 flight. Second, the Wright Flyer needed a rail to take off. So, Brazilians give credit for the airplane’s invention to Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew his 14-bis biplane near Paris in the autumn of 1906. He did so in public with Aéro-Club officials on hand to measure it, and he took off on his own wheels.

Wikipedia doesn’t come down on either side. It has a whole article for the rival claims, where the Wrights and Santos-Dumont have to share the page with Gustave Whitehead, Samuel Langley, and a few other men who were absolutely, definitely first.

2. Alan Turing cracked the Enigma code

In 2021, I wrote my book Mini Philosophy, and it was published with three mistakes. First, I wrongly claimed Christopher Nolan directed The Joker. (It was Todd Phillips.) Second, I attributed a quote to Aristotle that actually came from a scholar of Aristotle. But the third mistake, by far and away, was the one that caused the most uproar. I got emails, letters, and pretty intense direct messages. I had claimed the British had cracked the Enigma code. It was Alan Turing and the geniuses of Bletchley Park, surely? That’s what I’d grown up with.

But Enigma was first broken in Warsaw at the end of 1932 by a 27-year-old Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski. That’s almost seven years before the war began. He and his colleagues, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, spent the 1930s reading German messages. Then, in late July 1939 — five weeks before the invasion of Poland — they invited British and French codebreakers to a forest outside Warsaw and showed them how it was done.

None of this is a secret. Rejewski’s Wikipedia page sums up what he is known for in a single line: “Solving the Enigma machine cipher.” And GCHQ’s own history is happy to say that the first British Bombe owed a great deal to Turing’s meeting with Polish codebreakers. Turing was still a genius, but he was also standing on Polish shoulders.

I mean, really, this fact isn’t so much “disputed” as just “Jonny, you were wrong.”

3. There are seven continents

I kind of knew all the other facts on this list before researching this article, but this one was a shock. Seven. There are seven continents. I admit there’s a bit of controversy around “Australia” vs. “Australasia” vs. “Oceania,” but we all agree on seven, right?

But in Greece and much of the Romance-speaking world, from Lisbon to Lima, children learn that there are six continents, because North and South America are a single continent called “America.” Russian children learn six as well, but a different six: The Americas stay apart, but Europe and Asia are merged into Eurasia. Something a lot of anthropologists and geologists do as well. And the Olympic flag has five rings for five inhabited continents — one America again, with Antarctica left off altogether until the penguins whip together a bobsled team.

The Wikipedia article doesn’t pick a winner. There are, it says, up to seven continents and as few as four. Which means that somewhere, right now, two perfectly well-educated adults are arguing in a pub about something they each learned before they could tie their shoelaces. And they’re both right.

4. The United States won the War of 1812

That depends on who you ask, and in this case, there are three people you could ask.

Ask a Canadian, and you’ll hear about a plucky Canada seeing off an American invasion. Ask an American, and it’s the “Second War of American Independence.” Ask a Brit, and you’ll mostly get a blank look because, for Britain, it was a sideshow to the real business of beating Napoleon. And we’ve loved to hate the French ever since.

In a 2009 poll, 37% of Canadians said Canada won, and only 9% gave it to the United States. Not every American would argue. “By my count,” the American historian Donald Hickey said, “we lost the War of 1812, and we lost Vietnam.”

And Wikipedia? Its editors have spent years on the question. There is a dedicated discussion page titled “Who Won?” and then there was a formal mediation case. And after all that, the article settles on calling the entire debate “inconclusive.”

5. The Second World War began in 1939

On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. “This country is at war with Germany,” the British Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, said at the time. And so, that’s when the Second World War started.

But in Russia, the war that matters — the “Great Patriotic War” — began on June 22, 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In China, it starts much earlier. In 2017, the Ministry of Education announced that the war against Japan would be counted from 1931, not 1937, and an 8-year war became a 14-year war overnight.

Wikipedia keeps a whole archive of editors arguing about this, and at one point, the article itself cited 1937 as the start. My favorite contribution comes from an editor who backed 1939 on entirely practical grounds: They said that if Wikipedia said 1937, a teenager somewhere would copy it into their homework and be marked wrong.

Which is, I think, the whole point. So often, the “right” answer is simply the one your teacher is expecting. But both the teacher and the student are stuck in the same problem. As Georg Hegel, Jimmy Wales, and Pink Floyd all knew, we are all just fish swimming in a fishbowl, and no one’s commenting on the water.

This article The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Reflections on the Life in Perspective Book Tour
items.summary: A few days ago, I got back from my first official book tour for the launch of my new book Life in Perspective . I’ve traveled to promote my past books, but going on a proper book tour across three cities was something altogether different. In every room and conversation, I…
items.author: Tiago Forte
items.contentHtml:
A few days ago, I got back from my first official book tour for the launch of my new book Life in Perspective.

I’ve traveled to promote my past books, but going on a proper book tour across three cities was something altogether different. In every room and conversation, I could feel the anticipation and momentum behind the release of this book. There was a buzz in the air centered around this physical artifact that represented my best contribution to the world of personal development and inner work.

Here are my reflections on how it went and what I took away from it.

Los Angeles

First stop was Los Angeles, near where I grew up in Orange County. I hosted a book signing at The Last Bookstore, an ominously named shop that I felt alluded to the endangered state of reading in our attention-starved world.

The bookstore is in a repurposed bank, complete with a working vault packed with books, an amusing metaphor for knowledge as wealth. Towering columns, which I assume once conveyed trust and timeless authority, framed the main space where my event took place:

I had no idea how many people would show up for something like this, and was pleasantly surprised to greet around 25 attendees. About 7 of them were my family, and it was gratifying to be able to share this aspect of my work with them.

I had designed the agenda around one principle: What can we only do in person, not online?

I spent about 15 minutes talking about the book, what it was about, and how it came into existence. I explained how it connected to and addressed the gaps in my prior books. Then I led everyone through an embodied exercise demonstrating the book’s techniques in miniature form. Finally, I answered questions, and then signed books.

I’ve hosted a number of meetups in different cities before, and I’m always amazed at how people from my past will come out of the woodwork to meet me. At this event, a fellow Apple Store employee from when I worked there in college 18 years ago showed up, and we reminisced about our formative memories.

I met Azul Wells, who had taken my BASB course years ago and been inspired to start his own YouTube channel, which is now the leading channel on the subject of retirement with over 50 million views last year alone. I’m at a loss to even begin wrapping my head around the ripple effects of ideas I shared years ago that I think of as being in my rearview mirror.

The next day, we hosted the Annual Review Virtual Summit, welcoming several thousand attendees from all over the world to talk about the transformational impact of annual life reviews. I interviewed 10 guests chosen for their unique approach to structured reflection, and we all gleaned so many insights from what they shared.

As I set off for the next stop of my tour in San Francisco, my daughter gave me a small token of good luck – my book in miniature. A good reminder of how deeply the way I work influences my children, for whom it forms their model of what work is and means.

San Francisco

Flying to San Francisco felt like a homecoming in many ways, since most of the ideas I’ve written about and taught originated there.

Descending toward SFO airport, I gazed silently at my book lying on my fold-down table, thinking about everything that had happened to bring me to this moment – the failures, the heartbreak, the mistakes, the fear. I teared up, realizing that it was all the necessary groundwork to be able to create this system that so many people could now benefit from.

I recorded an interview with my friend Liz Moody for her podcast, and really enjoyed her witty and slightly irreverent take on the subject. As I talk to people outside my niche, I’m learning how universal reflective practice is, and yet how many different ways there are of understanding and practicing it.

I took BART to Powell St. station in the heart of downtown San Francisco, and as I was ascending the escalator to street level, I had a powerful wave of deja vu. I realized this was the exact elevator I’d used in March 2012, when I moved to the city to start my first job.

I was filled with the memories of uncertainty as well as excitement I felt at the time, striking out on my own in the big city to seek my fortune. In this picture I took at the time, I look like a kid:

Back then, I remember emerging out onto the bustling street on a beautiful sunny day, surrounded by tourists waiting for the trolleys that turn around on that spot. I emerged to find an identical scene greeting me this time as well.

I remember trudging up the street to the cheapest Airbnb room I could find. So cheap, in fact, that it had bedbugs, and I had to throw away most of my things almost as soon as I arrived.

I walked up the very same street toward Union Square, and was taken aback to notice my book through the glass, on display at The Best Bookstore where my signing would take place.

It told me I was known here, I was welcome here, and that there were people waiting to receive me this time. There I was again, 14 years later in the exact same spot, but now in such a different situation.

I checked in to my hotel and, a few hours later, headed back to the bookstore to start the event. Again, to my pleasant surprise, there were around 24 people who showed up, including some who I’d worked with on past books or courses.

I passed the microphone around and asked people where and how they’d encountered my work, and it ran the gamut from YouTube to my blog, from recent content I’d created on AI to some of my earliest writing on the Theory of Constraints. The crowd reflected the eclectic and sometimes meandering path I’d taken to get here.

I had a free day in San Francisco for the first time in a long time, and decided to go on a walk around town.

I visited the American Bookbinders Museum, which documented in fantastic detail the many, many innovations that took place across history in just one narrow aspect of bookmaking – the process of binding the pages.

Comparing the dirty, labor-intensive, error-prone process of the past with the totally seamless process of today, I felt grateful for all the obscure inventors who’d worked so hard to make one tiny step just slightly more efficient.

Visiting the SF Museum of Modern Art, I was struck repeatedly by prominent quotes on the walls that seemed highly relevant to the topic of my book, a reminder that any given work is part of a long lineage of thinking and feeling.

New York City

If San Francisco represented my past, and Los Angeles my present, then flying to New York felt like voyaging into the future. A wider horizon for where my ideas could lead me.

I did a book signing at Powerhouse Books on Columbus Circle, with around 26 people in attendance, with my friend Ryder Carroll as the moderator. Once again, they came from all over the region, from all walks of life, with such different relationships to me and my work.

The following days were filled with less public, but no less meaningful events. I attended an author’s dinner hosted by Alex & Books, where we talked for hours about our respective journeys through the publishing world.

I visited the 9/11 Memorial Museum and was amazed that such an extensive collection could be assembled to commemorate one single day in history. This quote from Virgil jumped out at me as a reminder that history can be created in a day, but not erased in a day.

I visited the offices of Simon & Schuster, my publisher, in Rockefeller Center for the first time. It felt like entering the inner sanctum of the literary world, towering above the streets of midtown Manhattan. My editor for this and the last two books, Stephanie, welcomed me.

We talked about the current and future state of publishing. I came away with the sense that they think on much longer timescales than the current worries around the supposed “death of reading.” People have worried about the decline of reading for centuries, but I think it’s doing just fine.

I walked through Times Square a couple of times, and as always was amazed by the buzzing proliferation of so many competing ideas, movies, Broadway shows, products, newscasts, and perspectives. They all compete on the level playing field of the Internet now, I realized, as do I. There are no commanding heights or privileged gatekeepers anymore, just a free-for-all on the global attention landscape.

I ended the trip with a visit to Bathhouse, a chic sauna in Williamsburg like something out of ancient Roman times, with my friend Ryder. The view of the Manhattan skyline from the rooftop pool was the perfect closing scene to a whirlwind trip.

The feeling I’m left with is that it all matters. It matters that writers spend years putting their best effort and thinking into books. It matters that people read those books and spend time immersed in new ways of seeing the world. The relationship between those two groups is one of the most precious parts of our culture in a world of increasingly fragmented attention, and I want to spend my career helping to strengthen it.

Most of all, I want to say an enormous THANK YOU to the hundreds of people who were part of creating and launching this book. Writing books is truly the furthest thing from a solo effort. It’s a community effort, and I’m immensely grateful to be part of such an interesting and supportive one. I’ll take that gratitude into my own annual review starting shortly!

items.title: Big Time Off: The Transformative Power of Sabbaticals and How to Take One
items.summary: I recently shared that I’m starting to plan an epic multi-month road trip down the length of South America with my family, which I’m dubbing “ Operation Gallavant .” As I’ve begun digging into the details, it’s quickly become clear to me that the single biggest challenge isn’t…
items.author: Tiago Forte
items.contentHtml:
I recently shared that I’m starting to plan an epic multi-month road trip down the length of South America with my family, which I’m dubbing “Operation Gallavant.”

As I’ve begun digging into the details, it’s quickly become clear to me that the single biggest challenge isn’t going to be the travel logistics, homeschooling, or anything like that. It’s going to be taking months off work.

I know some long-term travelers work on the road, via Starlink or Internet cafes. But I knew right away that I didn’t want to do that. Having three young kids in tow makes it almost an impossibility, and besides, what’s the point of road-tripping if I’m just going to be stuck on my computer?

I want to be totally, 100% present during our South American overlanding trip, not even checking my emails on the margins or ruminating on my projects in the back of my mind. Which means that it’s slowly dawned on me that I’m going to be taking a sabbatical. That word snuck up on me, an implication unexpectedly popping out of my other plans.

It was serendipitous that, just as I was considering all this, a new book appeared on my desk addressing exactly this topic: Big Time Off, by DJ DiDonna.

It’s the culmination of years of work by an organization he founded called The Sabbatical Project, which aims to spread awareness and acceptance of sabbaticals as an essential part of modern work life.

I read the book with an eye toward my own future sabbatical, and here’s what I learned that has made the biggest difference for me.

The research

One of the first things DiDonna discovered as he set out to understand sabbaticals was that little research existed on the topic. He had to conduct his own.

Through a series of studies, he found that sabbaticals alleviated burnout, increased creativity, improved relationships, and helped people reinvent themselves. Remarkably, the people he studied described their sabbaticals as “peak life experiences” on par with their wedding day or the birth of a child.

The language that kept arising in his research was that taking several months off of work allowed them to “feel human again.” The day-to-day work routine has a tendency to inflict a continuous storm of “slings and arrows” on our psyche. Perhaps none of them deal a crippling blow, but the gradual accumulation weighs on our soul.

Sabbaticals are a way to unburden it.

In his research, DiDonna found that only about 50% of couples who are fifty today can expect both partners to be mentally and physically able to travel extensively by the time they reach retirement age. That’s an astonishing finding when the standard attitude is “we’ll travel when we’re retired.”

The single best predictor of a person’s likelihood of taking a sabbatical is whether they know someone who has taken one. Thus, Big Time Off is full of stories of real people who took the plunge. These stories are some of the most potent raw material to begin constructing your own version of what it could look like.

Most of these stories weren’t from people who were in crisis. But they also didn’t possess so-called “post-economic” wealth. They were mid-career, with both successes and failures under their belt, and often with kids. They had to draw most of all on their creativity and imagination to carve out the sabbatical months.

This was perhaps my biggest takeaway from the book: that a sabbatical doesn’t have to be a shining mountain that you reach “one day,” when you’ve figured everything out and achieved all your goals. It is a project like any other, and you can make it happen much earlier with some ingenuity.

The origins

The word “sabbatical” comes from the old Hebrew šabbat, or Sabbath, referring to the weekly day of rest deeply ingrained in Jewish culture. You can think of a sabbatical as a Sabbath not for a week, but for a much longer timescale of years.

The first official sabbatical policy was created at Harvard in 1879 for the purpose of “health, rest, study, or the prosecution of original work in literature or science.” This extended break from their usual teaching duties was essential to allow academics to collaborate with their European counterparts, who tended to take summers off.

After experimenting with different periods of time off, Harvard settled on a full year of paid leave, which has remained the norm today, 150 years later. Within 40 years of its creation, fifty top universities had adopted similar policies. From academia, the practice slowly started spreading to the corporate and governmental sectors.

Fast forward to today, sabbaticals are becoming an increasingly common and accepted life stage. The number of American employees who are on sabbatical at any given time has tripled in just the last five years according to The Sabbatical Project’s surveys. Younger workers are twice as likely to take a sabbatical as older generations. Hiring managers are beginning to view it as a positive life choice and a sign of lifelong learning and growth.

Why take a sabbatical

DiDonna spends much of his book persuading the reader to take the possibility of a sabbatical seriously, even if it seems out of reach.

He notes that we tend only to take extended leave when it’s forced on us – in the form of a health emergency, being laid off unexpectedly, or during a downturn in our industry or the economy. But this approach is like waiting to go to the dentist until you need a root canal. Much better to do regular cleanings.

A sabbatical is an intentional process of planning, saving up, and making space for a break on your own schedule, on your own terms, to serve the purpose of your own choosing. It’s the act of pushing back against the incessant demands for productivity and progress and prioritizing your long-term personal growth instead.

Two of the most cited changes among sabbatical takers are increases in perspective and confidence. What could be more important for you to gain more of mid-career, when facing some of the most consequential, high-stakes decisions that will shape the latter half of your working years?

A sabbatical is a gift you give yourself. The gift of stepping back to see your life clearly, from a wider longer-term perspective, while you still have time to make major changes. It’s the rejection of your professional identity as the only identity that matters.

DiDonna recommends taking at least 6 months off for a sabbatical, which represents a little more than 1% of the typical 40-year career. I think it’s a small price to pay to align the remaining 99%.

Functional workaholism

I was struck by DiDonna’s definition of “functional workaholism,” which he said was a common condition that led people to take a sabbatical. He described it as “an ongoing state of gradually deteriorating job engagement, efficacy, and personal health.”

This is different from burnout. It’s the slowly accumulating background stress that, if left unchecked, eventually leads to burnout.

He tells the heart-wrenching story of a high-achieving law partner whose firm offered sabbatical policies:

“He and his son had always dreamed of hiking part of the Appalachian Trail together, but when his son graduated high school, the father was close enough to a major promotion that he skipped his sabbatical. Four years later, he’d achieved his career goals, but his son was too busy starting his first job out of college to join the hike. It wasn’t an acute tragedy, but it was a pretty big missed opportunity.”

I see myself in these portraits of the functional workaholic so clearly.

On the surface, everything looks fine, or even great. I work reasonable hours, on projects of my choosing, with broad autonomy, and make great money. I spend lots of time with my family, friends, and on exercise and hobbies.

This would be an enviable position for many, and I’m not complaining.

But there are small signs: the compulsion to work on weekends and on vacation, not because I have to, but because it’s when I feel most alive and engaged. It’s the coping mechanisms of caffeine, sugar, and social media I find myself turning to to eke out a little more productivity from an aching body. It’s the moments playing with my kids when my mind is elsewhere, or I feel too tired to give them the attention they need.

None of this is anywhere close to an emergency. I could easily keep going this way forever. No one would notice anything amiss, and many would even admire me for this relatively laid-back lifestyle. But there is another state I’m looking for, that I’ve occasionally tasted: when my work doesn’t always get the best of me.

This has made me realize that I’m scared of the boredom, the lack of feeling useful, and the absence of visible progress that stepping back from work will entail. But I’m also curious to know: who am I apart from the role I’ve played as an entrepreneur, founder, and CEO?

The opportunity for the business

Besides changing my personal relationship with my work, the other big opportunity I see is to reshape the nature of my business.

I started my career enamored with the ideas of Rich Dad, Poor Dad, the promise of “passive” income, and the siren song of “evergreen” information products that could be sold while I slept. I saw the hard-grinding careers of older generations and wanted nothing to do with them.

But over time, the idea of letting systems do work on my behalf faded into the background. The pandemic exploded our revenue and opportunities, and it felt only natural to chase those opportunities with everything I had.

The last 6 years have flashed by, and it feels like that whole time I’ve been in “wartime mode,” pushing and striving and maximizing growth, when my essential nature is more that of a wandering artist.

I see a chance to redesign Forte Labs in such a way that it can withstand my absence, and thus justify starting to wander again. And I know that won’t happen until I’m truly absent for a long stretch. I’ll need to invest a lot more authority and autonomy in the team, redesign our educational programs to not rely on me as the sole instructor, and focus more on existing products that can be incrementally improved, whereas I tend to favor wholesale new creations.

One of the most intriguing aspects of the book was that DiDonna doesn’t recommend necessarily abstaining from all forms of work during a sabbatical. The goal is not to sit on a beach sipping from a coconut the entire time. That could be maddeningly boring, especially for those who enjoy thinking, learning, and efforting.

Instead, the intention is to do a different kind of work than you’re normally used to. To break the usual pattern, and thus explore a new aspect of your identity or develop a new interest. That could be building a deck if you normally work at a computer all day. Or taking a class and becoming a student in a new field. Or dedicating oneself to a community service project or important cause.

Without a boss evaluating your performance, or a fixed set of responsibilities to uphold, or the demands of company politics, you’re free to redefine your relationship to work as something intrinsic and freely chosen, not just an obligation.

DiDonna writes: “…until you’ve left your life behind, you cannot truly change; you’re stuck with a foot in the old world. If you’re going to take a journey, commit.”

In a company setting, taking a sabbatical is a helpful opportunity to reveal the full scope of an employee’s responsibilities. Rather than their work piling up on their desk or in their inbox until they get back, that work has to be transferred to others. That provides a chance to unpack what’s necessary and what’s not, and to develop resilience toward turnover.

I’ve always known that I am the bottleneck to the company’s growth, and my sabbatical will give me a chance to test what it would look like to remove it.

Three archetypes

DiDonna describes three archetypes of people who take sabbaticals. Many tend to be a mix of more than one.

The Achiever views their sabbatical first and foremost as an achievement; that is, an opportunity to get things done. They often use external markers – like mastering a new language, writing a book, or completing a long trek – to mark their progress. The pitfall is that they can use these projects to avoid looking inside and examining their true desires. If this is you, the greatest use of a sabbatical might be to take a break from this mindset itself.

The Seeker is someone who grapples with uncertainty and often goes on a journey of some kind to resolve it: either physically, like traveling to see friends or family or inspiring places, or spiritually, voyaging into their inner world. Seekers set out to find answers to their most deeply held questions. Their pitfall is that they can hold unrealistic expectations about the depth of the transformation they experience.

The Explorer mainly wants to find out what’s out there in the world, and is less concerned with the practical application of what they find. This may involve time away from home, backpacking or road-tripping, or exploring a stack of books. Their intention is to widen the aperture on what’s possible. The potential pitfall could be that their sabbatical lacks intention and focus.

Protean careers

The rise of sabbaticals has coincided with a shift in the nature of modern careers. DiDonna dubs it the “Protean career,” because it’s no longer enough to climb a predefined ladder step by step – you now have to regularly reinvent and reimagine your career, much like Proteus, the shape-shifting sea god of Greek mythology.

Lifespans are also getting longer, and therefore, so are career spans. Our forties and fifties are no longer the twilight of our working lives; they may be only a halfway mark with decades left to come. That means more chances to pivot toward a new role, or even a whole new career.

Many of our careers are now entrepreneurial by necessity, which demands a deeper, more creative approach. We alone are in charge of our direction, our choices, and the fulfillment (or lack thereof) that we derive from our work. The playing field of possible options is vaster than ever, and the landscape is more uncertain and quickly changing than any previous generation knew.

A sabbatical can be understood as a strategic rehearsal and insurance plan to step back and redirect your career strategically, instead of waiting for it to be forced upon you. It’s less about specific skill acquisition and more about gaining the perspective and courage you’ll need to face the future proactively.

The connection to annual life reviews

While reading Big Time Off, I was struck by the many parallels to my own teaching on annual life reviews, as recounted in my new book Life in Perspective.

DiDonna writes:

“Living in alignment requires recurring adjustments over the course of your life, informed by who you are, how you’ve changed since the last time you checked, and clarity about who you want to be.”

I couldn’t agree more! In a way, I think an annual life review is a mini version of a sabbatical, geared toward many of the same intentions but occurring on a 12-month rhythm.

I see many ways these two structures can be complementary – the annual review gives you a pre-scheduled time to revisit and reflect on the year, while the sabbatical is its heavier-duty cousin for when you need to step back even further, and take even more time, to dig into the depths of your identity.

Both rituals are a chance to intentionally answer the question, “Who am I, apart from the roles I’ve played?”

The post Big Time Off: The Transformative Power of Sabbaticals and How to Take One appeared first on Forte Labs.
