items.summary: Please enjoy this transcript of a different kind of episode . For a change, I’m the one in the hot seat. I was interviewed on stage by Zuhairah Washington, a senior vice president at Zillow . There were a lot of questions around AI, how to be robust or anti-fragile in a…
items.author: Tim Ferriss
items.contentHtml:
Please enjoy this transcript of a different kind of episode. For a change, I’m the one in the hot seat. I was interviewed on stage by Zuhairah Washington, a senior vice president at Zillow. There were a lot of questions around AI, how to be robust or anti-fragile in a fast-changing world, why booking a mini-retirement forces you to fix your systems, fear-setting, why I try to diversify my identity, the books I’ve reread the most, and much, much more. You don’t need to be in real estate to use any of it.

Books, people, tools, and resources mentioned in the episode

Legal conditions and copyright information

Listen onApple Podcasts
Listen onOvercast
Timeless Principles for Fast-Changing Times — Asymmetric Bets, Effectiveness Over Efficiency, Identity Diversification, and The Books I Keep Rereading

Additional podcast platforms

Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts, , Overcast, Podcast Addict, Pocket Casts, Castbox, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Audible, or on your favorite podcast platform.

Transcripts may contain a few typos. With many episodes lasting 2+ hours, it can be difficult to catch minor errors.

Zuhairah Washington: Before I dig into the concepts in it with many people raised their hands being familiar with many of your books, I thought it’d be good to ground us in before you were an author, when you were running a business, BrainQUICKEN, a sports nutrition company. If you could take us back to that time and you found yourself just working 14-hour days, you couldn’t unplug.

I think in short you said instead of you running the business, the business was running you. And when I read that, I just thought that story has to resonate with some people in this room. Raise your hand if so, who feel that way. And the first question I wanted to ask is what was the first thing you actually automated your way out of?

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, flashback. So we go back in time. The first thing I’ll say is that if you’re a working dog, meaning a lot of people are probably border collies in the audience, got to run them or they’re going to chew on the couch. I’m one of those. So the fixing the compulsion to work to fill the void is something you need to revisit. I think a lot of people are just hardwired that way. In terms of automation, the question of what to automate I think is very much on the forefront of people’s minds right now because of AI. And I think it’s a very good question, but there are a few questions that helped me in asking first.

And the framework in The 4-Hour Workweek roughly, I won’t get too deeply into this, but it’s D-E-A-L. So you have definition, elimination, automation, that’s step number three, and then liberation, which we probably won’t spend a ton of time on right now. But what I first did that opened the door to eliminating and then automating was looking at A, how I was spending my time, but more specifically looking at an 80/20 analysis applied to my customers. So a lot of my time was spent chasing wholesale accounts, distributors. The world was my oyster, but that was the problem. If you have infinite optionality, you are dead in the water. And what I realized pretty quickly is that I was spending almost all of my time on the high-maintenance, low-yield customers.

Zuhairah Washington: Wow.

Tim Ferriss: And I was letting the best customers coast because they were so easy to deal with. And once I had that written down in front of me in concrete terms, it became very clear that I should focus on increasing order volume, repeat purchases, et cetera, with the critical few instead of doing what I thought I should do, which is fill my waking hours doing the hard work on this vast majority who constituted the trivial many. So that was important to first lay as a groundwork, but the actual definition of that first step refers to defining what you want your life to look like because in the absence of that, the push and the pressure to grow your business in abstract terms can take over everything. So I’ll give just a couple of resources up front.

Zuhairah Washington: Please. That’s what people want.

Tim Ferriss: The 30 minutes is going to be so fast. So the more things are changing—and things have never changed faster—that’s going to accelerate the more I try to focus on things that don’t change very much. There are certain constants. Definitely grab a copy of The Effective Executive by Peter Drucker. This is an old book. And the reason I mention that is because doing the right things matters a lot more than doing things well. So picking your targets, that is one I would start with.

The second thing I would mention is if you search my name and Dreamlining, kind of like I guess the aircraft, but Dreamlining, that’ll pull up something, you don’t have to spend any money on this, that allows you to define in concrete terms what you want to do, be, and so on in financial terms. And that gives you then, based on your ideal lifestyle or what you think is your ideal lifestyle, a target monthly income. And once you have that, then you can start to, back of the napkin, work out how you would address those critical few to get to that TMI.

And the reason that this TMI, target monthly income, not too much information, although I’ll probably do that too, is that if you don’t have that, you leave yourself very vulnerable to a lot of human foibles and inclinations that served us very well thousands of years ago, don’t serve us so well now. I’ll just riff for another second. Eliminating is the core piece. I think Drucker is the one who said there’s nothing so pointless as doing something well that should not be done at all. That is what AI allows you to do all day long. And I use these tools, my team uses these tools, I’ve invested in a lot of these companies. It’s an accelerant, it’s a magnifier, but it can be the magnifier of the meaningless. So you have to be very cautious for that. So define, eliminate, and then automate.

In terms of the first things I automated, it was a lot of supply chain and process-related stuff. And that might not seem immediately applicable to real estate, although a little known fact, my dad was a real estate broker for decades. I got to see it up front and personal. It’s always been hard. It’s always had great opportunities. I think that will continue to be the case. And with the automation, all that comes down to fundamentally is writing down what you do. And there will be a point in the very near future where you will be able to actually use these SkyNet monsters to your benefit, meaning LLMs and so on, where they’ll capture a screen flow. They’ll watch you work for a few hours and they will identify exactly what you do.

And then at that point you can get a list and whether it’s through delegating to people, whether it’s through using agents and so on, you will be able to automate a lot, but it should be the very few things that you’ve identified move the needle and are Archimedes levers that point you towards that target monthly income. I’ll stop there for now.

Zuhairah Washington: Wow, you painted a future there and you gave so much detail and I hope you guys wrote down the book recommendations, but that future where someone just watches what you do and then that becomes a process—

Tim Ferriss: Can I give one more tip?

Zuhairah Washington: Go for it.

Tim Ferriss: I’m going off script here. One more is just because everyone in this room may identify with real estate. I’ve actually also even—lesser known fact—been involved with real estate on some level, but the skills that you have, the tools that you’ve developed, in many cases, transcend that. And chances are a lot of you did something else before and you may do something later. A really useful trick that I have found is use a tool like Wispr Flow. It’s a dictation tool. Stick your AirPods in, go for a walk for coffee, talk about what you’re worried about, talk about what you think you might want to do, talk about the constraints in your business, talk about the pressures, just riff for like 10 minutes.

Stop every two minutes to let it catch up because it’d be a bummer if you lost the 10 minutes. Put that in a note on your phone. That’s where this will all be captured. Put that into, copy and paste it into ChatGPT, Claude, pick your LLM, and ask it what you should do next based on what it knows about you. Say, “Three to five years in the future, what might I want to aim for?” It is remarkable the type of intel and insight that you’ll get back. And that can help point you towards what types of skills you want to develop so that you feel like you have a safety net of transferable skills that you can point at any different type of future that might emerge.

Zuhairah Washington: It’s such a great point. I remember a few months back someone saying oftentimes people use AI with specific tasks. They use it like a search engine when in fact they should use it more like a strategist. And what you’re talking about, which is just talk to it like someone on your board or an advisor and then ask, “What should I do next?” and level up that conversation. It’s such a great insight.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah. Two followups on that. One is I would uncheck the default box that says, “Use my information to train the model.”

Zuhairah Washington: Yes.

Tim Ferriss: However, number two, you’re not just pulling from the quote-unquote “memory” of this LLM of what you’ve put into it. You’re pulling from everybody else. It is incredible the type of insight you can get back. And that’s literally 10, 15 minutes of effort. It is a strategist in your pocket. Just like Waymo is the most experienced driver in the world. In some senses, these things are the most—I think OpenAI is probably getting close to a billion users. Take advantage of that.

Zuhairah Washington: All right. Well, with that, I want to transition to asking you a question that was submitted by one of our participants here. We asked a few attendees who submit questions. So this is the first one. It’s from Jeremy Ruff of Garrett Realty Partners in Virginia Beach. And he is on pace to do 50 deals this year, going to 80 next year, but surprise, surprise, Jeremy feels like he’s the bottleneck. Every call, every contract runs through their phone, even on vacation with their parents.

And right now Jeremy is really afraid that if he doesn’t pick up the phone, that he’ll lose a deal. And so the question is, what’s the first thing you’d advise Jeremy to cut, automate, or hand off in the next 90 days? And what’s the smallest test they can run to prove their business can survive a week without them before they take their dad on his bucket list trip to Alaska in May?

Tim Ferriss: All right. Let’s see.

Zuhairah Washington: Very specific.

Tim Ferriss: I am excited about this one because I’m going to start with the last portion of that.

Zuhairah Washington: Okay.

Tim Ferriss: So the last portion is that trip. I would argue, and I’ve seen this hundreds upon hundreds of times now, from people who are kind of 9:00 to 5:00 with something they clock in and out of, to CEOs you would recognize. I think one of the most powerful things that you can do, which is a, it’s a forcing function for a lot of really durable change, is take a mini-retirement. That’s a term I used in The 4-Hour Workweek. But an example, a shorter example of this would be this one week trip with his dad. Ideally make it two to four because then you can’t—two to four weeks, that’s right, because then you can’t act as a firefighter and come back to a whole mess and try to clean it up.

You actually have to, and this is the point of the exercise, you have to improve your systems. You have to do the defining and eliminating. You have to automate certain things. You have to perhaps empower people you haven’t fully empowered before, before you leave. And then when you come back, yes, you will have small bad things that have happened. You might have some larger bad things that have happened, but the systems that you’ve put in place are the types of things that allow you to go from 50 deals to 100 deals, to 200 deals, to 300 deals.

Whereas if you look at your current way of doing things, you might be able to manage 80 deals by yourself, but let’s just say you get what you want and you’re successful. This is a very important question to ask. What happens if you’re the dog who catches the car? What then? So what happens if you win the game? If you win the game, you have more deals and you can telescope out three or four or five years and see that inevitably it’s going to break. It’s not sustainable. I’d say there are two other things that I would add to that.

So the first is, what I’m suggesting is going to sound terrifying, understandably, to a lot of people. Before I did it the first time, it was also terrifying. Took me a long time to bite the bullet. There’s an exercise called fear-setting. I did a TED Talk on it. You can find it for free. I don’t want to take up all of our time right now talking about it, but that allows you to take the emergency brake off. And it’s very similar to goal-setting, but it’s called fear-setting. You can find it very easily online. The last thing I would say is that it’s very helpful to practice quote-unquote “poverty.” Now everyone here is in the global one percent of affluence and agency. That’s great news. And you live in the land of opportunity.

That is the United States for sure. But as my friend and others have done, Kevin Kelly, founding editor of Wired Magazine, for a week a year, he’ll just camp out in his front living room in a sleeping bag. You can do this with your kids and he’ll have shitty—I’m from Long Island, sorry—instant coffee and oatmeal and beans and that’s it. Cost you, I don’t know, $10 a week for food. And you’ll realize how liberating that can feel and how even if you hit bumps, even if you lose that one deal, even if you lose 10 deals, even if you lose 25 deals, you lose half your current deal flow. I’m making some assumptions here, right? But if that allows you to create systems that lay the groundwork for getting to 100, 150, 200 deals, that’s a great trade. You should take that all day long.

So those are a few things that I would add. In terms of what to cut and so on, it’s such a personal question because it depends not only on your business goals, but your personal goals and perhaps family priorities and things like that. But what I’ve just mentioned, I think are more or less universally useful. And the benefit of that one decision, book the trip to Alaska, pay for it, invite your dad, apply all of this very, very helpful sunk cost. People think of sunk cost as a bad thing. Sometimes it’s really helpful. Now your ass is on the line. And if you can make it two weeks, make it two weeks. That will change your life. It will prove to you that the sky will not fall when you do it, but you’re going to have to do some very hard thinking and maybe a little heavy lifting in advance.

Zuhairah Washington: I love that. Okay. Another question from Shoshana Hogg with Mogul Real Estate in Temecula, California. Her question is, “In a culture obsessed with optimizing, automating, and scaling, what do you think never should be optimized and where does the push for efficiency actually disconnect us from what matters most?”

Tim Ferriss: Yeah. Efficiency and optimizing are over-applied, I would say, which might sound funny considering that I wrote all these books about optimizing various things. But if you were to watch me kind of day to day, like a nanny cam in my house, you’d be like, “What is this guy doing?” It’s like a broken Roomba and we’re roaming around the house. “He forgot his socks three times on the first hour. What is this guy doing?” And the reason that I can get away with that, this is nothing new, I’ve always been like that, I think, is that I’ve been very careful and that Effective Executive book by Peter Drucker lays it out very eloquently. Effectiveness is doing the right things. Efficiency is doing things right.

Always focus on choosing your targets first. And I would say that that’s the starting point. And if you start with the targets, you can actually do a very C+ job, but if you’re better at picking these asymmetric bets, and I’ll define that, you have a lot of margin for error and you have a lot of margin for the unexpected in the future too. So what I mean by that is asymmetric bet is something where you really cap the downside, but you have a lot of upside potential. And I’ll just give more book recommendations. Losing My Virginity by Richard Branson is a great read. Great book, full of adventures. I’m sure it dates very poorly, but I read it a long time ago.

And his reputation is this of an incredible risk-taker. Bets the farm, does all this craziness and it’s a great brand. I’m sure you’ve seen him windsurfing or kite boarding with a naked lady on his back. It’s like, “Okay. All right, Richard.” However, he’s actually really focused on mitigating risk. And if you study how he started Virgin Atlantic, for instance, the question wasn’t, “How can we beat British Airways?” I’m writing about this right now. The question was, “How do we make the downside so minimal that it’s worth taking a chance?”

And he cold called Boeing and negotiated the most insane deal structure you could ever imagine, limited employment and lease terms and everything to one year. He could sell the plane back to Boeing at the end for the original cost if needed. I mean, he basically made it risk-free, all upside. And you can start to look at your life that way, and the mini-retirement would be a good example of this. Did I miss anything in that question? I might have.

Zuhairah Washington: No, you’re on it. The piece that may be doubling down on is what disconnects us where efficiency can disconnect us from what matters most?

Tim Ferriss: Well, there are a lot of ways that it can be disconnecting because efficiency is a blunt instrument, if that makes sense.

Zuhairah Washington: Yeah. Well said.

Tim Ferriss: It can give us a false sense of progress because we’re improving at doing something regardless of what that something is. And I’ll give you a very concrete example. I have a friend who was asking me about how he can use AI to improve A, B, and C, and one was writing. And I gave him my answer and the piece of my answer that he had not figured out; this is one of the top AI researchers and safety researchers in the world. There’s something called HackerOne that ranks kind of pay for bounty hackers. They get hired by companies and he was recently ranked at number one, just to give you an idea, this guy knows what he’s doing.

And the piece that was missing is I said, “If you’re going to use A, B, and C to draft two different versions that have very different tones of what you wrote, only ask for two versions. Do not ask for five versions. If you ask for five versions, it’s going to create infinitely more work for you than just writing it from scratch.” But that is in search, that Faustian bargain is in search of an efficiency that is an efficiency at surface level, but ends up creating more work. And I would say that, I think it was Oliver Burkeman in Four Thousand Weeks, another great book. These are my greatest hits books, by the way. These are books every book—

Zuhairah Washington: Hope you guys are writing these down.

Tim Ferriss: Every book I’ve mentioned, I’ve reread at least four or five times. Awareness by Anthony de Mello, probably 50. But the disconnect and the thing that he mentioned was priorities, as a plural, is a relatively new thing. I had no idea. It was priority, etymologically, for a very long time, one thing. So I think, and this may tie into some of what you heard earlier about identity and cognitive dissonance with identity, past, present, hopefully future. You need to know what your one priority is.

Zuhairah Washington: It’s a hard one.

Tim Ferriss: I think we’ll probably come back to that, so I’ll stop there. But it’s like, if you could only choose one thing, and this comes down to picking targets, what is it? Is it business? Is it your son or daughter? Is it your spouse? Is it something else? Is it some mental health issue that is actually the riskiest thing, the biggest landmine in your life or in someone you love? What is that one thing? And getting very clear on that, not forever, but for the next one, two, three, six months, I think clarifies a lot, makes decision making a lot easier.

Zuhairah Washington: A lot of what you say sounds reasonable on paper, read the book, set the one priority. Oftentimes though, we stand in our own way, right? And I could see some folks in the room saying, “Okay, Tim, what I’m hearing you say is that you’re challenging many of us to rethink about how we ourselves feel that we add value. There’s some things that we should be deprioritizing and oftentimes when we need to automate or make something that’s more efficient that we feel deeply tied to our own self-worth, it can be hard to let that go. So what advice would you have to push through that?”

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, I’ll sound like a broken record for a second. The first is that one book that I said I read basically every year, at least once, probably twice, Awareness by Anthony de Mello, The Perils and Promises of Reality was the initial subtitle, helps you to become aware of the stories and the beliefs that govern your life because everything else is downstream of that. And it could be around identity, right? I am an X. I am a Y. And there’s a very famous startup figure named Paul Graham. He co-founded something called Y Combinator, which helped produce Dropbox and Reddit and Airbnb and all these companies.

And he writes these short little essays. A lot of them are very good. One of my favorites is, I think it’s “The Top Idea in Your Mind,” but another, “Maker’s Schedule, Manager’s Schedule.” But he has one on labels and he basically says the more labels you apply to yourself, the dumber you become. Now, if I were being a little more generous with it, I’d say the more you artificially constrain yourself and create a very fragile vessel.

So number one, if these beliefs and kind of reactive patterns that we have are governing your life, you have to be able to see those. So Awareness is a very great place to start as a book. And then I would say secondly, something that I’ve done repeatedly in my life, because what I did when The 4-Hour Workweek came out is very different from what I did five years later, which is very different from what I do now, is just like you would do with your portfolio perhaps, if you like your stocks and your bonds and your cash and your this and your real estate and that and whatever, you might diversify. Why? Because you don’t want everything to be correlated and crater or concentrated in a way that could go to zero. All right. I actively try to look for identity diversification plans.

Zuhairah Washington: Interesting.

Tim Ferriss: It’s a very fancy way of saying if your self-worth is tied into, say, the growth of your business and it’s become very concentrated, that is psychologically very risky. So you can create a sense of progress in other areas. I’ll give you an example. For me right now, I’m doing a lot of rock climbing. I’m not good, right? It’s like I’m built like a snowman. It’s like a Coke can getting dragged up a wall. It’s not a goal of mine to get to the Olympics, but I really enjoy it and I’m making a lot of progress with coaches. It’s not expensive.

If I have a bad day writing, I have an 870-page book that I cut down to 350, this thing has been taking forever. Very proud of it. I think it’ll be good, but I can have a brutal week if I don’t have another siloed asset, in this case rock climbing, an activity where I can make progress, my entire self-worth can plummet and I can go into this recursive spinning. So I would say try to, I would strongly recommend, it doesn’t need to be something that takes up a lot of time. Exercise, by the way, like Richard Branson, I once had a chance to, I met Richard, I interviewed him later, but the first time I met him, I was on Necker Island, of course, and I was starstruck and someone asked him, they’re like, “Richard, if you give one advice to people who want to become more productive, what would it be?” And he was like, “Work out every day.”

Zuhairah Washington: Wow.

Tim Ferriss: “It gives me three to four more hours of productivity every day.” It’s like, “Okay, great.” So with my example, the rock climbing or whatever, it’s a multiplier for everything else. And you can pick two or three of those, but that would be another recommendation. It’s just like, do not let your identity become completely concentrated in one thing if you can avoid it. I’ve just seen too many people crash and burn.

Zuhairah Washington: Yeah. The identity is a big one. All right. I have two more quick questions.

Tim Ferriss: Can I say one more thing about identity?

Zuhairah Washington: Yes, you can.

Tim Ferriss: A really easy way to kind of force that to converge with the one priority that I was mentioning earlier is think about all the labels you might apply to yourself, right? So it could be business owner, it could be mother, it could be, fill in the blank, come up with a list and then ask yourself, if you could only choose one of these labels, which would it be?

Zuhairah Washington: You continue to push us to prioritize and choose.

Tim Ferriss: Right. But it’s like if you choose mother, that means if you have a high maintenance customer or prospect who might convert into a great sale, but you’ve committed to, say, a family dinner or a family outing and this person says, “I can only do it at 7:00 p.m.,” what does that mean? It’s a hard thing. Life is trade-offs. It means you say no to that person. And I wish I could give a magic bullet that made everyone happy and everyone reasonable, but that doesn’t exist. It’s all trade-offs. And now the alternative is what’s the cost? If you take that call, you are still making a trade off.

Zuhairah Washington: And that changes. That can change over time.

Tim Ferriss: It can change and it does change over time.

Zuhairah Washington: Yeah.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah.

Zuhairah Washington: Okay. So if an agent walked out of this room today and did one thing to start protecting their most important hours, what would you tell them to do before they go to sleep tonight?

Tim Ferriss: I’m going to go back to my notes. I trust the pen more than I trust my memory. So besides all the various things that I’ve already listed off, I would say even if you don’t have a trip to Alaska, book that mini-retirement, it really is the one move, the one domino that tips over a lot of others automatically. I would say a few others that are easy to do, right? If someone’s going to do something like tonight, okay, if I’m on the spot for that, I would say consider using a tool like Freedom. There’s an app called Freedom. It’s been around for a while. Freedom.to. It will block your social media. It will block the things that are distractions because for all of those platforms, their customers are advertisers. You are the product. Your attention is the product. So I would say block those.

I haven’t had social media apps on my phone for five years, probably. Trust me, it’s like 10 years of free therapy. And if you still need to use social media for your life, fine. Just do it from your laptop. You can take all your photos and videos and then transfer it to your laptop. It applies a little—friction can be your friend. You can use it that way. Another one is, I’m going to double down on the fear-setting as an exercise. The last thing I’ll say is consider archiving any emails that are older than six months old. Maybe it’s three months old. And then you can very quickly identify your most common contacts. You could archive all of their email and then text or call them and ask them if there’s anything they’re waiting on you for. And that’ll leave you with fewer emails.

And from there, I would stop making your inbox your to-do list because then you’re reopening email, you’re like, “Oh, God, I have to come back to that. Mark it as unread. Oh, wait, I forgot to do that. Now I thought I read it and it’s a disaster.” Sam Corcos, who runs a company called Levels, he has a whole system for this, but basically go through your inbox and be like, all right, if this is going to take two minutes, just reply to it. If it’s going to take 30 minutes for me to reply to this, put it in your calendar. If this is going to take 15 minutes, put it in your calendar. And that way you shift the to-do list from your inbox to your calendar. And everything I just mentioned can be accomplished within a few hours. So that’s something people could do tonight or tomorrow.

Zuhairah Washington: Love it. Okay. So last, last question.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah.

Zuhairah Washington: I brought my original copy of The 4-Hour Workweek. Would you sign it for me?

Tim Ferriss: Yes, of course.

Zuhairah Washington: Thank you.

Tim Ferriss: That is an original copy too. I can tell by the color, this is early, early days.

Zuhairah Washington: I think it’s 2007?

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, 2007. Back when I was white knuckling a little faux-hawk that I had left.

Zuhairah Washington: I should have read the bio in this one.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, this is early days. This is first edition, 33rd printing. Yeah. Crazy. Crazy.

Zuhairah Washington: Yeah. Thank you, Tim.

Tim Ferriss: Yeah. Thank you so much. All right. Thanks everybody. Really appreciate you having me. Good luck.

Zuhairah Washington: Thank you.

items.title: Anthropic IPO fails to prevent a tech stock wipeout
items.summary: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Just like taking your high school sweetheart out to Dave and Buster’s wasn’t enough to save the relationship, Anthropic’s record $2 trillion IPO couldn’t reverse the unraveling of the AI trade. Tech stocks came crashing down yesterday—including…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Just like taking your high school sweetheart out to Dave and Buster’s wasn’t enough to save the relationship, Anthropic’s record $2 trillion IPO couldn’t reverse the unraveling of the AI trade. Tech stocks came crashing down yesterday—including shares of Anthropic, which plummeted 8.5%, at one point nearly hitting its IPO price of $83.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq nose-dived 5.6%, wiping out its gains for the year, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.7%, putting it in bear market territory.

AI anxieties didn’t go anywhere

Despite hopes that Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO signaled renewed investor appetite for the AI industry, jitters remain following Jensen Huang’s scandal-prompted resignation from Nvidia, which led to tightened US chip export controls.

Plus, many investors are skeptical about the costly AI infrastructure binge and worried that higher interest rates could temper borrowing by AI hyperscalers. And they anticipate regulation by newly elected Democrats when they take office in January that would slow the data center buildout:

  • Chipmakers were the hardest hit in yesterday’s rout, with shares of AMD, Intel, and Broadcom sinking 13%, 8%, and 12%, respectively. Nvidia dropped 14% after federal regulators said yesterday they were probing its accounting practices.
  • Shares of AI developers shoveling cash into data centers, like Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon, also sank.

Locking in gains? In recent weeks, institutional investors sold AI stocks, which analysts say is consistent with the common practice of taking profits before the end of the year. Investors appear to be rotating out of tech stocks into less risky sectors, propelling the S&P 500 consumer staples index up 0.68% and boosting government bonds.

Looking ahead…some analysts note that tech companies might be trading at a discount since their projected earnings are still strong, with the current price-to-expected-earnings ratio being the lowest since 2020, per FactSet. As for Anthropic, retail investors’ appetite for its shares will be clearer when its options start trading on Monday.—SK

items.title: Forget method acting. Hollywood is method dressing
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc., Photos: Getty Images Throughout the press tour for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , the film’s stars have been “method dressing”—donning styles that pay tribute to the project they’re promoting. And while it’s been a popular marketing tactic in…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Throughout the press tour for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the film’s stars have been “method dressing”—donning styles that pay tribute to the project they’re promoting. And while it’s been a popular marketing tactic in recent years, some critics say it’s starting to feel like the trend’s swansong. That’s fitting, because the Hunger Games outfits feature a lot of plumage (check them out here if you don’t believe us).

When did method dressing start? Geena Davis helped get the ball rolling in 1992, wearing a dress with baseball stitching on it to the premiere of A League of Their Own. Other celebrities grabbed the baton, like Zendaya, who wore a cobweb dress in 2021 at the premiere of Spider-Man: No Way Home and tennis outfits to promote Challengers in 2024.

I’m a Barbie girl: But the trend’s current iteration exploded in pink in 2023, when Margot Robbie went full Barbie-mode to promote her theatrical turn as the famous doll. Turning the movie into a cosplay event helped propel it to a $160+ million domestic opening weekend.

Three-finger salute? Though some critics think method dressing is getting stale, in part because the guys still tend to wear normal clothes, it has managed to generate buzz for the new Hunger Games movie (this article included).—BC

5-Bullet Friday

The latest from author and investor Tim Ferriss

Hi All!

Welcome to a very special holiday edition of 5-Bullet Friday!

I dislike shopping, but I do love finding the perfect gift. Alas, damn adults seem to have everything or need nothing. So… If you’re having trouble thinking up great options, below are a few goodies that deliver.

I use all of these products on a daily or weekly basis. I’ve also recommended each to my close friends and family.

I also reached out to some of my favorite companies to get special deals for subscribers. Each sponsored bullet is indicated with a star at the end of it, just like this sentence.* Literally everything I mention below lives in my home somewhere, including the sponsored gems.

Happy holidays to you and yours! 🙂

The most Japanese thing on my mind

Hibi Box of 30 Incense Matches (Amazon, Ameico, Urban Natural). Thanks to the inimitable writer Dan Levy, perhaps best known as David Rose on Schitt’s Creek, for introducing me to these via “10 Things Dan Levy Can’t Live Without | GQ.”

Air purifier I’m loving

Jaspr Air Scrubber. I’ve tried a lot of air purifiers over the years, and there are a handful of great options. This is the best combination of function and aesthetics that I’ve found. I love the design and am buying more units for my family. It’s quiet enough to sleep next to, and it’s beautiful enough to put in your living room. Thank you to Dr. Tommy Wood for introducing me to Jaspr.

Supplement I’m taking every morning

Momentous Creatine. I’ve relied on Momentous for years, and they’re my default because I trust them with sourcing, testing, and labeling. Their creatine is a daily staple. I typically aim for five (5) grams per day, both for cognitive function and the well-studied effects on strength and muscle. Their upgraded creatine is 99.99% pure, manufactured in a pharmaceutical facility, and screened for heavy metals, microplastics, and PFAS. If you take anything daily, you need to have complete confidence in purity.

Like all Momentous products, their creatine is NSF Certified for Sport®, meaning independently tested for purity, safety, and label accuracy. For an early Black Friday, save 40% on your first subscription order with code BFCM, which you need to apply at checkout.*

Book I’m gifting

Seeing Silence: The Beauty of the World’s Most Quiet Places by Pete McBride. The sublime is easy to find in this book, whether you simply flip through the gorgeous photos or do a deep dive into the prose. Pete McBride, a National Geographic photographer and filmmaker, shot the images across all seven continents, from Everest to Antarctica. The foreword is by Bill McKibben, a renowned environmentalist and journalist. The prologue is by Erik Weihenmayer, the first blind person to summit Everest.

Tiny gadget in my backpack

Sennheiser Pro Audio Condenser Microphone. This lav mic plugs straight into a USB-C iPhone and makes on-the-go recordings sound much better than any built-in laptop or phone mic. It’s remarkable what quality you can get, especially if paired with the Ferrite app that allows you to record high-fidelity audio straight on your iPhone.

Book that I’m rereading and gifting

Art Is the Highest Form of Hope. Special thanks to the amazing Susan Cain for sending this beautiful book to me, which is full of bite-size philosophy and much-needed imagination. These days, a little light goes a long way. From the description: “Advice, strong opinions, and personal revelations by the world’s greatest artists—exclusively researched for this new book.”

Sleep technology I’m using

. I’ve been sleeping on an for years, and the new Pod 6 is the first version where the hardware fully gets out of the way, with a Hub that’s 50% smaller than the Pod 5. The new thermal engine reaches your set temperature 20% faster, and the cover includes 9x more biometric sensors for tracking sleep stages, HRV, heart rate, and more. Autopilot takes those signals and automatically adjusts the bed’s settings throughout the night, creating optimal conditions for better sleep. Members report up to 34% more deep sleep and a 32% average increase in sleep quality scores. It’s also a great gift for couples. Each side runs independently, so if one sleeps warm and one sleeps cool, everyone can be happy. The Pod 6 , the lowest starting price in the product’s history. Go to to save $700 on the Pod 6 and Base in Queen, King, or Cal King. Eight Sleep currently ships within the USA, Canada, the UK, select countries in the EU, and Australia. This special offer is valid through November 30. Individual results may vary.*

One pan I use for nearly everything

has become the one pan I use for practically everything, and it is my go-to in the kitchen. Its patent-pending NoCo® technology creates a coating-free, nonstick effect and is made without PFAS (including PTFE and PFOA), lead, and cadmium.

With a titanium interior, an aluminum core, and a stainless-steel exterior, you get the high-heat searing of stainless or cast iron with the easy release of nonstick. now offers this same technology across its full Titanium Pro Cookware sets. Their Black Friday/Cyber Monday event is the perfect time to try them. . Go to to take advantage of this special offer. With a 100-day trial, you can try it completely risk-free.*

How I’m finally getting in more Zone 2 cardio

M3i Studio Indoor Bike | Keiser. I’ve tried a lot of stationary bikes, including very fancy indoor trainers, for getting in Zone 2 cardio and VO2 max training. I hate nearly all of them. This M3i is not fancy, but it does allow me to elevate the handlebars enough so that (1) I’m not bumping my thighs into my stomach like a one-hour Heimlich maneuver, and (2) it doesn’t make my low back incredibly grumpy. The controls are simple, it’s durable, I don’t use an app with it, and, so far, it’s the only indoor bike that I’ve used consistently. And more good news: it’s found in a lot of commercial gyms.

Set-it-and-forget-it robot vacuum I’m loving

Matic. This is the closest thing to a house that cleans itself. It’s quiet enough that you forget it’s running, and it’s smart enough to leave your charging cables alone. The reviewers agree: WIRED gave it a rare 10/10, and to quote The Verge, “This WALL-E-like bot fixes the stuff every other robot vacuum gets wrong.” When I asked my audience on social media about Matic, the response was euphorically positive, and I got a flood of texts from 10+ friends who are converts. Fans include Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, my friends Kevin Rose and Naval Ravikant, and many others. Matic sold out last Black Friday, so order early. Go to MaticRobots.com/Tim for $400 off the Matic Serene Bundle or $300 off the Matic Bundle. Order before November 30th for delivery before Christmas (U.S. only).*

Tool that’s always on me

ProBody Pilates Ball. Yep, it’s a Pilates ball, but I don’t use it for Pilates. I keep it deflated in my backpack, and if I need lumbar support or butt padding anywhere on the road (in hotels, restaurants, airplanes, etc.), I give it literally 2–3 puffs of partial inflation and voilà! Deflated, this is small enough to fold up and stick in a jacket or jeans pocket.

What I’m drinking in the mornings

Brodo Bone Broth. Broth is one of the easiest ways to get quality protein and nutrition first thing in the morning. For the past two months, I’ve been having 1–2 Brodo packets per day, often simply poured into a mug and microwaved for 60 seconds. Brodo was founded by Chef Marco Canora, who was one of my primary teachers in The 4-Hour Chef. Marco is the real deal. He won a James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York City, which is like winning an Oscar in the food world, and he has plenty of other awards and accolades to boot. My favorite flavors so far are Tuscan Sun and Tom Yum, which are included in their sampler box.

Headphones I’m loving for music while working and writing

Focal Bathys wireless, noise-cancelling headphones (Headphones.com, Amazon, B&H). These are my current default headphones if working at a coffee shop or busy co-working spot.

A grab bag of fun recommendations

The Way. This is an easy one. I’ve explored a lot of meditation practices over the years. My current hands-down favorite, and the easiest way to get back in the habit, is The Way, taught by Zen Master Henry Shukman. Here are 30 days for free, no credit card required.

Premium MGO 1000+ Mānuka Honey from Manukora. I love this smooth and creamy Mānuka honey. I sometimes use it before bed to help with sleep, combined in hot water with a bit of apple cider vinegar. The exact recipe is courtesy of the late Dr. Seth Roberts (2 tablespoons of apple cider vinegar and 1 tablespoon honey, stirred into 1 cup of hot water).

Coyote the card game (46% off), which I co-created with Exploding Kittens. If you have any kids or relatives aged 8–15, you can start playing—and laughing—in minutes. Think charades + hot potato + brain fun.

Awareness: Conversations with the Masters by Anthony de Mello. Nonfiction, 184 pages. I’ve gifted this at least 50 times, so I’ll keep gifting it.

And there you go! 17 of my favorite things that make great holiday gifts. I love them all and hope you do too.

Have a wonderful weekend and wonderful holiday season, everyone!

Much love to you and yours,

Tim

One pan I use for nearly everything

The Titanium Always Pan Pro from Our Place has become the one pan I use for practically everything, and it is my go-to in the kitchen. Its patent-pending NoCo® technology creates a coating-free, nonstick effect and is made without PFAS (including PTFE and PFOA), lead, and cadmium.

With a titanium interior, an aluminum core, and a stainless-steel exterior, you get the high-heat searing of stainless or cast iron with the easy release of nonstick. Our Place now offers this same technology across its full Titanium Pro Cookware sets. Their Black Friday/Cyber Monday event is the perfect time to try them. Get 29% to 43% off popular Titanium Pro cookware sets and free shipping on orders $135+. Go to FromOurPlace.com/Tim to take advantage of this special offer. With a 100-day trial, you can try it completely risk-free.*

How I’m finally getting in more Zone 2 cardio

M3i Studio Indoor Bike | Keiser. I’ve tried a lot of stationary bikes, including very fancy indoor trainers, for getting in Zone 2 cardio and VO2 max training. I hate nearly all of them. This M3i is not fancy, but it does allow me to elevate the handlebars enough so that (1) I’m not bumping my thighs into my stomach like a one-hour Heimlich maneuver, and (2) it doesn’t make my low back incredibly grumpy. The controls are simple, it’s durable, I don’t use an app with it, and, so far, it’s the only indoor bike that I’ve used consistently. And more good news: it’s found in a lot of commercial gyms.

Set-it-and-forget-it robot vacuum I’m loving

Matic. This is the closest thing to a house that cleans itself. It’s quiet enough that you forget it’s running, and it’s smart enough to leave your charging cables alone. The reviewers agree: WIRED gave it a rare 10/10, and to quote The Verge, “This WALL-E-like bot fixes the stuff every other robot vacuum gets wrong.” When I asked my audience on social media about Matic, the response was euphorically positive, and I got a flood of texts from 10+ friends who are converts. Fans include Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, my friends Kevin Rose and Naval Ravikant, and many others. Matic sold out last Black Friday, so order early. Go to MaticRobots.com/Tim for $400 off the Matic Serene Bundle or $300 off the Matic Bundle. Order before November 30th for delivery before Christmas (U.S. only).*

Tool that’s always on me

ProBody Pilates Ball. Yep, it’s a Pilates ball, but I don’t use it for Pilates. I keep it deflated in my backpack, and if I need lumbar support or butt padding anywhere on the road (in hotels, restaurants, airplanes, etc.), I give it literally 2–3 puffs of partial inflation and voilà! Deflated, this is small enough to fold up and stick in a jacket or jeans pocket.

What I’m drinking in the mornings

Brodo Bone Broth. Broth is one of the easiest ways to get quality protein and nutrition first thing in the morning. For the past two months, I’ve been having 1–2 Brodo packets per day, often simply poured into a mug and microwaved for 60 seconds. Brodo was founded by Chef Marco Canora, who was one of my primary teachers in The 4-Hour Chef. Marco is the real deal. He won a James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York City, which is like winning an Oscar in the food world, and he has plenty of other awards and accolades to boot. My favorite flavors so far are Tuscan Sun and Tom Yum, which are included in their sampler box.

Headphones I’m loving for music while working and writing

Focal Bathys wireless, noise-cancelling headphones (Headphones.com, Amazon, B&H). These are my current default headphones if working at a coffee shop or busy co-working spot.

A grab bag of fun recommendations

The Way. This is an easy one. I’ve explored a lot of meditation practices over the years. My current hands-down favorite, and the easiest way to get back in the habit, is The Way, taught by Zen Master Henry Shukman. Here are 30 days for free, no credit card required.

Premium MGO 1000+ Mānuka Honey from Manukora. I love this smooth and creamy Mānuka honey. I sometimes use it before bed to help with sleep, combined in hot water with a bit of apple cider vinegar. The exact recipe is courtesy of the late Dr. Seth Roberts (2 tablespoons of apple cider vinegar and 1 tablespoon honey, stirred into 1 cup of hot water).

Coyote the card game (46% off), which I co-created with Exploding Kittens. If you have any kids or relatives aged 8–15, you can start playing—and laughing—in minutes. Think charades + hot potato + brain fun.

Awareness: Conversations with the Masters by Anthony de Mello. Nonfiction, 184 pages. I’ve gifted this at least 50 times, so I’ll keep gifting it.

And there you go! 17 of my favorite things that make great holiday gifts. I love them all and hope you do too.

Have a wonderful weekend and wonderful holiday season, everyone!

Much love to you and yours,

Tim

items.title: November 20, 2026
items.summary: November 20, 2026 Reader 🌍 Improved Lifelike Voices — Most of the Lifelike voices for languages like Spanish, German, Chinese, and Japanese were English voices reading that language. Tristan added 48 native voices across 15 languages, with new options for Italian, Turkish…
items.contentHtml:
November 20, 2026

Reader

  • 🌍 Improved Lifelike Voices — Most of the Lifelike voices for languages like Spanish, German, Chinese, and Japanese were English voices reading that language. Tristan added 48 native voices across 15 languages, with new options for Italian, Turkish, Swedish, and Hindi.
  • 🎚️ Improved Speed Slider — Dragging the text-to-speech speed slider only changed the speed once you let go. Artem made the speed change as you drag, in the Reader app and in the Readwise Books app, audiobooks included.
  • 🤖 Improved API Saves — Documents saved through the Reader API or the MCP server never got Ghostreader's automatic summary or tags, even with both settings on. Rasul made those saves follow your Ghostreader settings, just like documents you save any other way.
  • 📺 Fixed YouTube Transcripts — Some English YouTube videos came in with an Arabic transcript and summary because YouTube had auto-dubbed them, and some livestream replays saved without a transcript at all. Rasul made Reader pick the original English track and use the replay's captions, so new saves get the right transcript.
  • 📤 Fixed OPML Exports — Stricter feed readers rejected Reader's OPML export, because each feed was missing a name label and characters like & in feed addresses weren't encoded. Rasul fixed the file, so your exported feeds now open cleanly in any OPML app.
  • 🗞️ Fixed Reappearing Feed Articles — Deleting a feed article with a publish date in the future didn't stick, because it came right back on the next sync. Rasul made Reader leave those articles deleted.
  • 🔌 Fixed Reader API Lists — Listing documents through the Reader API could stop partway with "Error decoding document list results", because some documents reported a published date of 0. Tristan made those dates come back empty, so the whole list loads.
  • 🔤 Fixed CJK Table of Contents — In Reader on web, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean headings in the table of contents could show in a different style of characters than the document. Krzys gave the contents the document's language, so the headings match the text.
  • 📲 Fixed iPhone Duo Pages — On an open iPhone Duo, the two-page view in Horizontal pagination started the right page before the fold, so some text sat in the crease. Cam centered the pages on the hinge, in the Reader app and the Readwise Books app.
  • 🛜 Parsing Updates — Krzys improved how Reader handles documents from plato.stanford.edu, blog.cloudflare.com, news.google.com, zhihu.com, web.archive.org, dailytelegraph.com.au, simplywall.st, lesswrong.com, justin.poehnelt.com, bloomberg.com, theguardian.com, pluralistic.net, and substack.com.

Highlights

  • 🖼️ Improved Home Cover Stack — The cover stack at the top of Home drew every source as a book, so square art for podcasts, articles, and tweets got cropped and given a spine. Ibai redrew it to match our emails, with a larger front cover, and square art now keeps its shape.
  • 🗺️ Improved Daily Review Audio — Daily Review audio read every highlight in the same English voice, even highlights written in German or Chinese. Tristan made it switch to a native voice for each highlight's language, so they sound the way they're written.

Books

  • 🚗 NEW! CarPlay — You can now take Readwise Books on the road. On iPhone, Books shows up in CarPlay with your library, so you can play an audiobook or have an ebook read aloud, change the speed and voice, and save a highlight without picking up your phone. Thanks to Cam for building it. (Android Auto coming soon!)
  • 🔍 NEW! Library Filters — On iPhone and iPad, you can now filter your library by whether a book is readable, its format, where it was synced from, or your top authors. Quick pills like Purchased, Uploaded, Ebooks, and Audiobooks sit right next to the filter icon. Thanks to Artem.
  • 📗 NEW! StoryGraph Import — Thanks to Mati, you can now bring your StoryGraph library into Readwise Books. Connect it from Import Books or Settings > Integrations, and your Read, Currently Reading, To Read, and Did Not Finish books come over with your ratings, reviews, reading dates, and progress. StoryGraph import is in beta, so let us know if you have any feedback!
  • ✏️ NEW! Edit Book Details — An uploaded EPUB with messy metadata could land on your shelf titled with a string of random characters by "Unknown", with no way to fix it. For uploads that didn't match a book in our catalog, the ··· menu now has “Edit details”, where you can change the title, author, and cover. Thanks to Artem.
  • 📃 NEW! Page Curl — You can now turn pages with a page curl animation in Readwise Books on iPhone and iPad. Choose Horizontal pagination (Beta) in your reading settings, then switch on Page curl. New readers on an iPad or iPhone Duo start with both turned on. Thanks to Cam.
  • ❌ NEW! Cross-Post Deletes — Removing a book in Readwise Books left it on your Goodreads shelves. A new “Cross-post deletes” toggle in your Goodreads settings removes the book, with its rating and review, from Goodreads too. It's off by default, and Goodreads can't undo a removal. Mati also made the cross-posting switch on the import's success screen turn on all four options at once.
  • 💸 NEW! Publisher Specials — The Readwise Books store now has a Publisher specials row on its homepage and a full page of ebooks on sale, where you can filter by genre and sort by popularity, lowest price, or biggest discount. When you're signed in, an “On your shelves” filter shows just the deals on books you're tracking, and book pages show the regular price crossed out next to the sale price. Thanks to Tadek.
  • 🏛️ NEW! Publisher Pages — You can now browse the store by publisher. Tap the imprint name on a book page, or start from the publisher list, to see that publisher's most popular books, new and upcoming titles, top authors, and full catalog. Book pages also get a More from row for the same imprint. Thanks to Tadek for this one as well.
  • 💳 NEW! Refund Requests — Asking for a refund on an ebook or audiobook from the store meant writing to support. Tadek added the option to choose “Request a refund” on a paid order in your account's Orders page and add a reason.
  • 🎧 Improved Manual Audiobook Sessions — Logging an audiobook in a manual session meant converting your player's timestamp into 1x time yourself, and listening faster than 1x inflated the session. Thanks to Johannes, you can now pick the app you listened in and enter what it shows: a percentage for Spotify, Libby, and other players, or the time left for Audible and Apple Books, along with your speed and the audiobook's length.
  • 📸 Improved Photo Highlights — When you selected text on a page you photographed, your finger covered the drag handle, and highlights saved as soon as you tapped Next. Johannes added a magnifier and a raised handle, plus a review screen where you can correct each passage's text and add a page number and a note before saving.
  • 📚 Improved Now Reading Widget — The Now Reading widget for Readwise Books only showed the last ebook you opened, so a paper book you were tracking with manual sessions never appeared. Cam made the widget show your latest manual-session book and open session tracking when you tap it. Johannes also kept covers in full color on Home Screens set to Tinted or Clear, where they used to show as a white block.
  • 🔔 Improved Notifications — Clearing your notifications in Readwise Books previously meant opening them one at a time. Artem added a “Mark all as read” button to the top of the Notifications screen so you can clear them all at once.
  • 👤 Improved Profile Photos — Once you'd set a profile photo in Readwise Books, there was no way to remove it, and a private Goodreads profile could still have its photo imported. Rasul added “Remove photo” to the photo menu in Edit Profile, and Mati stopped importing photos from private Goodreads profiles.
  • 🔒 Improved Private Accounts — An invite link from a private account still previewed that person's book covers and latest reading session. Artem made those previews show a plain Readwise Books card instead. Tristan also added is_private to books in the Books API and MCP server, so your tools can leave out books you've hidden.
  • 📦 Improved Boox Installs — Boox devices without the Play Store had no official way to install Readwise Books. You can now download the Android app straight from readwise.io/books-apk. Thanks to Rasul.
  • ↩️ Fixed Reading Position After Jumps — After you jumped back in a book, for example to look at a highlight, the app could save that earlier spot as your reading position, so a session showed +0.5% when you'd read more than 3%. After text-to-speech, the “Return to reading” button could also stay hidden. Tristan fixed both, in Books and the Reader app, so your progress stays where you actually are.
  • 📶 Fixed Offline Images — Books only downloaded their text for offline reading, so most images, the cover, and custom fonts went missing without a connection. Artem made Books download the whole book when you open it, so images show up offline too.
  • 🅱️ Fixed Publisher Styles — Some EPUBs lost the publisher's bold on title pages and headings, and others painted callouts as solid blocks of color. Artem kept the bold and dropped the background fills, in Books and in the Reader app when you use the publisher's original styles.
  • 📝 Fixed Goodreads Reviews — Reviews imported from Goodreads could show leftover (view spoiler) links and raw spoiler markup, and editing an imported review in Books could overwrite the one on Goodreads. Progress you posted could also land on a book Goodreads still had as Want to Read. Mati fixed all three, and more of your Goodreads books now find their match in Books.
  • 🔗 Fixed Kindle Links — While you connected Kindle, tapping Conditions of Use, Privacy Notice, or a link inside a book replaced the sign-in page, with no way back. Mati made those links open in your browser, so you stay where you were.
  • 🔇 Fixed Overlapping Text-to-Speech — Opening a different book kept the previous book reading aloud. Artem made Books stop the old book's text-to-speech as soon as you open a new one.
  • 🤝 Fixed Follow Buttons and Dates — Profiles showed a plain Follow button even when that person already followed you, and reviews and comments from earlier years showed only the month and day. Mati made the button say “Follow back,” and older dates now include the year.
  • 📑 Fixed E-ink Contents — On E-ink screens, you couldn't tell which chapter you were in from the Contents list. Mati made the current chapter bold, so it stands out on any screen.
  • ⏲️ Fixed Manual Session Fields — In a manual session, the timer showed the clock even with “Show clock” turned off, and typing into a prefilled position like 68% added to it instead of replacing it. Johannes fixed both, so the timer and position fields work the way you'd expect.
  • 📱 Fixed iPhone Duo Controls — On the iPhone Duo, the back button, the review sheet's close button, and the weekly card on Home sat under the column with the clock and status icons. Cam moved the back button into that side column and kept the rest clear of it.
  • 🧭 Fixed Signing In on the Web — If you only use Readwise Books, signing in or resetting your password on readwise.io dropped you on a page about importing highlights. Cam now sends you to the Readwise Books store instead.

items.title: Apocalypse fears may be boosting Costco’s biz
items.summary: Nick Iluzada While everything else seemingly breaks down, the place you go to for free samples and toilet paper stays up. Costco is enjoying a panic-fueled sales bump following the Microsoft outage, the FAA ground stop, and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media,”…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
While everything else seemingly breaks down, the place you go to for free samples and toilet paper stays up. Costco is enjoying a panic-fueled sales bump following the Microsoft outage, the FAA ground stop, and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media,” the financial institution Mizuho reported this week.

It’s like March 2020 anxiety all over again, except add the looming fear of AI wiping us all out:

  • As of Sunday, 21 of Costco’s 26 high-end generator models were sold out, per Mizuho.
  • Before that, Costco’s comparable US sales (excluding gasoline) rose 11% to 12% in the last week of October, compared with 6% to 7% in the previous three weeks, Mizuho estimated.
  • Toward the end of the month, members bought more rice, canned food, water, paper goods, generators, and batteries than usual, Costco’s CFO told Bloomberg.

But…all this started two weeks before the recent spate of outages, after the UK government urged the public to stockpile goods in case of an emergency and the Pentagon reportedly called for military bases to have 90 days’ worth of supplies on hand. Those warnings followed a streak of cyberattacks last month that created the nickname “Black October.”

Zoom out: Mizuho expects prepper-minded shoppers to lift sales at Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Sam’s Club, too. Yesterday, Walmart noted a jump in purchases of propane, bottled water, and camping gear.—ML

items.title: Tech execs are trying to appeal to Democrats after years of Trump allegiance
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc., Photos: Getty Images Elon Musk, who led Trump’s DOGE team and has donated more than half a billion to Republican candidates, said at Wednesday’s DealBook Summit that he wasn’t MAGA. And Musk isn’t the only tech executive to backpedal recently to save face…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Elon Musk, who led Trump’s DOGE team and has donated more than half a billion to Republican candidates, said at Wednesday’s DealBook Summit that he wasn’t MAGA. And Musk isn’t the only tech executive to backpedal recently to save face after the midterms’ blue wave.

Musk said he felt “pretty foolish” donating $500 million to Republican candidates who lost during the midterms. The comments mark a change for Musk after his last few years of very public political spending and support. With the Democrats taking over the majority in the Senate and House, giving them new power to launch investigations, other tech execs are also talking differently:

  • Palantir CEO Alex Karp told Politico last week that he has been a Democrat his whole life, identifying as an “unhappy Democrat.”
  • He also said Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive,” although the company has received external and internal pushback over its immigration enforcement platform used by ICE.

A group of strategists told the Washington Post they are lobbying tech execs to rework their approaches to wooing communities and Congress after years of hands-off regulation from Trump and other Republicans.

The big flip. Beyond Congress, Silicon Valley’s leaders are scrambling to ingratiate themselves with Democratic governors across the country—especially since many winning candidates campaigned on pumping the brakes on the AI industry.—MM

items.title: Anthropic gets rock star welcome in public markets
items.summary: Charly Triballeau/Getty Images The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry. The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
The AI world’s ball drop took place in Times Square yesterday, where Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq with a 34% price pop in an IPO seen as a bellwether for the broader industry.

The AI lab that former OpenAI employees founded in 2021 instantly became one of the world’s most valuable public companies:

  • ANT hit brokerages around noon, trading at $111, or 34% above the $83 price set yesterday for a pool of preferred investors. It settled at $97 by the end of the day.
  • The company’s IPO raised a record $81 billion, breaking the $75 billion record set by SpaceX in its public debut in June. Anthropic also sold $26 billion in private shares.

Though Wall Street’s willingness to snatch up Anthropic shares showed enthusiasm about the AI trade, it didn’t propel other parts of the market. The tech-heavy Nasdaq closed down 2.2%, which some analysts say was caused by investors cashing out gains from the Anthropic IPO bump and renewed anxieties about chipmakers.

More yachts are coming to San Francisco Bay: There are likely 2,800 Anthropic employees with shares now worth $10 million or more, while 600 employees are likely to have stakes valued at more than $100 million, per investment platform Hill.com. A windfall is also coming for early backers like Lightspeed Venture Partners, Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, and a VC firm co-founded by Ashton Kutcher, which owns 0.5% of Anthropic.

As for the rest of us…analysts say thatreturns from Anthropic shares will hinge on how productive the tech makes its customers, its ability to compete with rivals, and whether it can grow revenue fast enough to justify spending $900 billion on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s IPO has intensified calls from lawmakers to regulate the industry.

Anthropic has goals beyond growing your 401(k). It has legally committed to prioritizing the good of humanity by developing safe AI systems, per its Public Benefit Corporation status. Experts say this could turn off some investors, since Anthropic’s definition of public good could conflict with profits.—SK

items.title: A Van Gogh painting sold for a record $190.4m last night
items.summary: Kobei Li/Getty Images Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The price blew past the artist’s previous auction record of $117.2 million from four years ago.

The sale almost didn’t happen

It proceeded only after the owner selling the painting reached an eleventh-hour deal with the heirs of the previous owners. Anonymous heirs to Samuel Fischer, who bought the painting in 1909, allege the painting was sold in 1936 because of financial difficulties forced upon the family’s business by the Nazi regime:

  • Sotheby’s initially claimed there was no evidence the painting’s 1936 sale was made under duress.
  • On Tuesday, the families reached an agreement so that last night’s sale could take place. Details of the agreement were not released.

The painting was one from a collection of 12 that went on the auction block. Sotheby’s estimated that the dozen would fetch $450 million collectively, but they only sold for $412 million.

The art market is having a legendary week. Total sales at three of the biggest auction houses, Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips, are expected to hit $2.4 billion this week. That would rival 2025’s sales for the whole year. The houses already brought in $6.8 billion in the first half of 2026, per Bank of America’s recent Art Market Update report.—MM

items.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is out, and it's the highest-rated game ever
items.summary: Rockstar Games Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI ” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI , the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time. It’s already the…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI, the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time.

It’s already the highest-rated game in history: GTA VI scored a site-wide best 99/100 on the review aggregator Metacritic. Bloomberg called the open-world game “a masterpiece,” the New York Times said it’ll “steal your heart,” and IGN’s reviewer described it as “the single most impressive video game I have ever played.”

All those years spent crafting the franchise’s new Bonnie-and-Clyde-in-Florida installment appear to have been worth the wait for publisher Rockstar Games. Amid earth-shattering (and possibly internet traffic-shattering) demand, the company may have already made back its entire development budget, which is believed to be between $1 billion and $1.5 billion:

  • Preorders surpassed $1.5 billion, Sensor Tower estimated, putting GTA VI hundreds of millions of dollars ahead of preorders for other recent big-name video game releases.
  • Some analysts think GTA VI will sell 40 million copies in its first four months, raking in $3 billion in revenue, Bloomberg reported. For context, the highest-grossing movie in the world, Avengers: Endgame, made $2.9 billion.

Expect a ghost town today. Schools around the world anticipated empty classroom chairs, and time-off requests are ~20% higher today than usual, according to the workplace software provider UKG. Logitech gave its 7,000 employees the day off to explore GTA VI in all its alligator-quarreling, canine jet-skiing, and insurance-scam side quest glory.

Even if you don’t plan on playing…

…you’re still living in the GTA VI entertainment economy. According to Sensor Tower, over the next month:

  • Other games could see a 10% collective drop in players.
  • Streaming movies and TV shows might get 6 million fewer hours of playtime in the US.

Meanwhile…food delivery services, music platforms (the game has a 30-song original soundtrack) and livestreamers are expected to cash in.

Farewell, GTA V. In preparation for GTA VI, GTA Online players bid adieu to the franchise’s beloved fifth installment last night with a peaceful “last ride” through Los Santos.—ML

items.title: What’s causing all the tech outages?
items.summary: Niv Bavarsky If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated cyberattack.

It’s AI’s fault…sort of. Anthropic and OpenAI have released AI models that can detect exponentially more bugs than a human could ever find. That’s created a race between organizations trying to close the holes and hackers looking to exploit them. The speed and volume of recent patches have caused some infrastructures—like the ones at Microsoft, Apple, and the NSA—to buckle. Experts believe more disruptions will happen as institutions continue to gain the tools to patch vulnerabilities.

In the case of the infamous ground stoppage last weekend, the FAA said the problem was traced to defective routers in Arkansas and Texas, although experts who spoke to CNET doubted the explanation’s plausibility and pointed to a new AI air traffic control system that rolled out nationwide shortly before the debacle.

Paranoia is understandable. Last month was dubbed “Black October” because of the high volume of cyberattacks—many done by a new AI hacking tool called Artex. On the Friday of the ground stoppage, the FBI released a warning about Artex, but a spokesperson later said that it was just a coincidence.—DL

items.title: Who’s going to profit from Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO?
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US economy.

The company will officially price its initial public offering today, before trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker “ANT.” The IPO will not be very ant-like: Anthropic initially set shares at $70 to $78 apiece, and at the top end of its pricing, it would raise $90.4 billion, with a valuation at $1.4 trillion. As banks closed share orders yesterday afternoon, orders were seven times the number of available shares, according to Bloomberg.

  • Anthropic’s share price could be over $80 today, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
  • That would mean a valuation as high as $1.6 trillion.

As the first major AI lab to go public, the IPO is viewed as a high-stakes stress test for both the AI industry and the entire global economy. A disappointing opening would still net investors huge gains, but it’d also add further fuel to ongoing AI skepticism.

Who’s set to gain?

For starters, the 300 or so investors who threw money at Anthropic, according to PitchBook. Some of the biggest venture capital funds are already preparing the champagne bottles: Menlo Ventures was in for $750 million in 2023. Lightspeed Venture Partners led a $3.5 billion round in 2025, and earlier this year, Sequoia, Greenoaks, and Altimeter joined private equity and corporate buddies to raise Anthropic’s largest funding round of $65 billion.

  • In the first half of this year, AI has snagged $355.9 billion from VC funds. That’s 86% of all US venture capital funding in that time frame, according to Clearstead’s analysis of Pitchbook data.
  • Because so much of AI development is concentrated in San Francisco, the city is taking in a third of all global VC dollars right now, according to PitchBook.

Who else is getting rich? An average Anthropic employee could see their equity balloon to $72 million. The company’s biggest customers, Amazon and Google, are set to own roughly 28% of Anthropic’s stock after the IPO.—MM

items.title: Jensen’s former employer reports stellar earnings
items.summary: Cheng Xin/Getty Images Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic relationships with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as two employees.

Financially, things look great. Revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter, and the company predicted it will grow 12% in Q4. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is boosting its 2028 growth outlook from 70% to 75%, giving investors hope that the chipmaker could persevere post-Jensanity. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading.

But things will be different:

  • Nvidia will stop selling certain chips to China, signifying a pivot away from Huang’s push to promote ties to the country.
  • Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” about supporting other AI companies, a sign it might retreat from its role as a financial backstop to the industry.

Jensen spoke out. In his first public statement since the ouster, Huang said earlier in the day that he’d be “honored” to return as CEO. But board chair Harvey Jones reiterated on the earnings call that that’s not being considered.

We’ll hear from him again: Huang will testify to Congress about Nvidia’s compliance with chip export controls on Dec. 1.—SK

items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Prediction markets are plagued by a reputation for being susceptible to insider trading. That’s why Kalshi enlisted Martha Stewart to star in a new ad warning potential customers about the consequences of rigging markets and the platform’s new safeguards against it.

The 90-second spot features Stewart—who was never convicted of insider trading but was found guilty of lying to investigators in a trading scandal—in a replica of the kitchen from her 1990s TV show preparing a pie but leaving out the ingredient of confidential information (it’s not the best metaphor).

Kalshi also announced it would follow the recommendation of an integrity committee to provide more tailored surveillance around markets depending on their risk profile. The company said that grouping marketswith similar insider trading risks together will “reduce false positives” and “focus review on higher-risk activity.”

Hours after the marketing blitz began, The Wall Street Journal reported that Kalshi is halting trading on markets that allow users to put money down on what words President Trump will say on a given date, after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ordered it to do so on Friday. The CFTC said it was due to the ease with which these markets could be influenced. In August, a White House teleprompter operator settled an insider trading case with federal regulators.—DL
